title: Non-Hermitian Mosaic Maryland model
summary: We introduce the non-Hermitian mosaic Maryland model, where a discrete modulation period and a non-Hermitian phase are incorporated into the potential, rendering the originally exactly solvable system generally non-integrable. This model provides a unique platform to investigate how structural modulation governs localization in complex quasiperiodic potentials. Using Avila's global theory, we analytically derive the exact Lyapunov exponent and obtain explicit formulas for the complex mobility edges. Remarkably, for modulation periods kappa >= 2, the system intrinsically hosts kappa-1 robust extended bands that persist independently of the potential strength and non-Hermiticity. We further characterize the topological nature of these phases via the spectral winding number. Unlike the standard Maryland model, the mosaic modulation induces mobility edges, and the resulting phase transitions are continuous, reflecting the non-integrable nature of the system. Numerical calculations of the inverse participation ratio and fractal dimension confirm the analytical predictions for the asymptotic form of the mobility edges in the large non-Hermiticity limit. This work establishes structural design as a powerful degree of freedom for engineering wave transport and enhancing the robustness of extended states in non-Hermitian systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a non-Hermitian mosaic Maryland model that combines structural modulation with non-Hermiticity, creating a non-integrable system with analytically derived mobility edges and robust extended bands.
AI.motivation: To investigate how structural modulation governs localization in complex quasiperiodic potentials and establish structural design as a powerful degree of freedom for engineering wave transport and enhancing robustness of extended states in non-Hermitian systems.
AI.method: Introduces the non-Hermitian mosaic Maryland model with discrete modulation period and non-Hermitian phase; uses Avila's global theory to analytically derive exact Lyapunov exponent and explicit formulas for complex mobility edges; characterizes topological nature via spectral winding number; performs numerical calculations of inverse participation ratio and fractal dimension.
AI.result: For modulation periods κ ≥ 2, the system intrinsically hosts κ-1 robust extended bands that persist independently of potential strength and non-Hermiticity; mosaic modulation induces mobility edges with continuous phase transitions; numerical calculations confirm analytical predictions for asymptotic form of mobility edges in large non-Hermiticity limit.
AI.conclusion: Structural design serves as a powerful degree of freedom for engineering wave transport and enhancing robustness of extended states in non-Hermitian systems, with the mosaic Maryland model providing a unique platform to study how structural modulation governs localization in complex quasiperiodic potentials.

title: Generative Inversion of Spectroscopic Data for Amorphous Structure Elucidation
summary: Determining atomistic structures from characterization data is one of the most common yet intricate problems in materials science. Particularly in amorphous materials, proposing structures that balance realism and agreement with experiments requires expert guidance, good interatomic potentials, or both. Here, we introduce GLASS, a generative framework that inverts multi-modal spectroscopic measurements into realistic atomistic structures without knowledge of the potential energy surface. A score-based model learns a structural prior from low-fidelity data and samples out-of-distribution structures conditioned on differentiable spectral targets. Reconstructions using pair distribution functions (PDFs), X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and diffraction measurements quantify the complementarity between spectral modalities and demonstrate that PDFs is the most informative probe for our framework. We use GLASS to rationalize three contested experimental problems: paracrystallinity in amorphous silicon, a liquid-liquid phase transition in sulfur, and ball-milled amorphous ice. In each case, generated structures reproduce experimental measurements and reveal mechanisms inaccessible to diffraction analysis alone.

AI.tldr: GLASS is a generative framework that inverts multi-modal spectroscopic measurements into realistic atomistic structures for amorphous materials without requiring interatomic potentials or expert guidance.
AI.motivation: Determining atomistic structures from characterization data is challenging for amorphous materials, typically requiring expert guidance or good interatomic potentials to balance realism with experimental agreement.
AI.method: A score-based model learns a structural prior from low-fidelity data and samples out-of-distribution structures conditioned on differentiable spectral targets, enabling inversion of multi-modal spectroscopic measurements without knowledge of the potential energy surface.
AI.result: Reconstructions using PDFs, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, and diffraction measurements show PDFs as the most informative probe. GLASS successfully rationalizes three contested experimental problems: paracrystallinity in amorphous silicon, liquid-liquid phase transition in sulfur, and ball-milled amorphous ice, reproducing measurements and revealing mechanisms inaccessible to diffraction alone.
AI.conclusion: GLASS provides a powerful generative framework for inverting spectroscopic measurements into realistic atomistic structures, enabling new insights into amorphous materials by revealing mechanisms that conventional diffraction analysis cannot access.

title: Geometric Classification of Biased Quantum Capacity via Harmonic Translation
summary: We establish an exact noise-model-derived characterization of quantum error correction under diagonal local phase noise. Under uniform locality, the maximal logical dimension under t-local phase errors equals Aq(n,2t+1), the classical q-ary packing function. Because no affine or stabilizer structure is imposed, nonlinear spectral supports achieve this bound and strictly exceed all affine constructions whenever Aq(n,2t+1)>Bq(n,2t+1). This follows from a harmonic translation principle: diagonal phase operators act as rigid translations in the Fourier domain, reducing the Knill-Laflamme conditions exactly to an additive non-collision constraint (S-S) cap Et={0}. For structured phase noise, exact correction is equivalent to independence in an additive Cayley graph, connecting biased quantum capacity to classical zero-error theory and the Lovasz theta function. Under mixed Pauli noise, simultaneous protection in conjugate domains incurs an intrinsic rate penalty R <= 1-(gamma_X+gamma_Z)/2, exposing a discrete harmonic uncertainty principle. In contrast with stabilizer- or graph-based frameworks, this classical correspondence is derived directly from the phase-noise model itself rather than from an auxiliary algebraic construction.

AI.tldr: Quantum error correction under diagonal phase noise is exactly characterized by classical q-ary packing bounds, with nonlinear codes achieving optimal performance beyond affine/stabilizer constructions, revealing connections to classical coding theory and a discrete harmonic uncertainty principle.
AI.motivation: To establish a direct, noise-model-derived characterization of quantum error correction under diagonal local phase noise, connecting quantum error correction to classical coding theory without relying on auxiliary algebraic constructions like stabilizer or graph-based frameworks.
AI.method: Uses harmonic analysis to translate diagonal phase operators into rigid translations in the Fourier domain, reducing Knill-Laflamme conditions to an additive non-collision constraint. Analyzes structured phase noise via additive Cayley graphs and connects to classical zero-error theory. Examines mixed Pauli noise to reveal intrinsic rate penalties.
AI.result: Maximal logical dimension under t-local phase errors equals classical q-ary packing function Aq(n,2t+1). Nonlinear spectral supports achieve this bound and strictly exceed affine constructions when Aq(n,2t+1)>Bq(n,2t+1). Structured phase noise connects to classical zero-error theory via Lovasz theta function. Mixed Pauli noise reveals intrinsic rate penalty R ≤ 1-(γ_X+γ_Z)/2, exposing a discrete harmonic uncertainty principle.
AI.conclusion: Diagonal phase noise enables direct classical correspondence for quantum error correction, with nonlinear codes achieving optimal performance beyond stabilizer constructions. The approach reveals fundamental connections between quantum error correction, classical coding theory, and harmonic analysis, exposing intrinsic trade-offs in protecting against conjugate errors.

title: Lamb-shift-induced switching of energy transfer in open quantum batteries
summary: Open quantum batteries (QBs) operate under unavoidable system-environment interactions, where both dissipation and coherent renormalization influence their performance. While most previous studies focus on dissipative effects, the role of environment-induced frequency renormalization, such as the Lamb shift, remains insufficiently explored.In this work, we investigate an externally driven QB composed of two coherently coupled quantum harmonic oscillators, representing the charger and the battery. By incorporating both dissipation and Lamb-shift corrections within a Lindblad master equation, we show that the Lamb shift effectively renormalizes the system eigenfrequencies and thereby modifies the resonance condition with the external drive. We demonstrate that tuning the driving frequency relative to the renormalized eigenmodes leads to a mode-selective energy transfer process, resulting in a controllable redistribution of energy between the charger and the battery. This behavior manifests as a switching of the dominant energy storage channel and can be quantitatively understood through a supermode decomposition of the coupled system. Our results clarify the dynamical role of environment-induced frequency shifts in open quantum batteries and provide a physically transparent framework for optimizing work extraction under realistic operating conditions.

AI.tldr: Lamb shift in open quantum batteries enables mode-selective energy transfer between charger and battery by renormalizing system frequencies, allowing controllable energy redistribution.
AI.motivation: Previous studies on open quantum batteries focus mainly on dissipative effects, while environment-induced frequency renormalization (Lamb shift) remains insufficiently explored despite its potential impact on battery performance.
AI.method: Study an externally driven QB with two coherently coupled quantum harmonic oscillators (charger and battery) using Lindblad master equation incorporating both dissipation and Lamb-shift corrections, analyzed through supermode decomposition.
AI.result: Lamb shift renormalizes system eigenfrequencies, modifying resonance conditions with external drive; tuning driving frequency relative to renormalized eigenmodes enables mode-selective energy transfer, leading to controllable redistribution of energy between charger and battery.
AI.conclusion: Environment-induced frequency shifts play a crucial dynamical role in open quantum batteries, providing a framework for optimizing work extraction under realistic conditions through controlled energy channel switching.

title: Contextuality as a Left Adjoint: A Categorical Generation of Orthomodular Structure
summary: Contextuality is widely regarded as a hallmark of quantum information, yet its structural origin is often obscured by probabilistic or operational formulations. In this work, we show that non-distributive orthomodular structure need not be postulated, but arises canonically as a left adjoint from classical Boolean contexts. We introduce a gluing functor that takes pairs of Boolean algebras and identifies only their minimal and maximal elements via a categorical pushout. The resulting lattice is orthomodular but generically non-distributive. We prove that this construction is left adjoint to a forgetful functor selecting Boolean subalgebras, thereby providing a free but constrained generation of quantum-logical structure from classical contexts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the failure of this pushout to remain Boolean is equivalent to the absence of global sections in the sheaf-theoretic framework of Abramsky and Brandenburger. This establishes a precise correspondence between contextuality as a sheaf obstruction and non-distributivity as a colimit failure. Our results offer a categorical and lattice-theoretic reconstruction of contextuality that precedes probabilistic notions and clarifies the structural necessity of quantum logic in information-theoretic settings.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that quantum contextuality arises canonically from classical Boolean contexts through a categorical gluing construction, establishing a precise correspondence between sheaf-theoretic contextuality and lattice-theoretic non-distributivity.
AI.motivation: To clarify the structural origin of quantum contextuality, moving beyond probabilistic or operational formulations, and to show that orthomodular quantum logic arises naturally from classical Boolean contexts rather than being postulated.
AI.method: Introduces a gluing functor that takes pairs of Boolean algebras and identifies only their minimal and maximal elements via a categorical pushout. This construction yields an orthomodular lattice that is generally non-distributive. The approach uses category theory and lattice theory to establish adjunctions between classical and quantum logical structures.
AI.result: The pushout construction produces orthomodular but non-distributive lattices, and this construction is proven to be left adjoint to a forgetful functor selecting Boolean subalgebras. The failure of the pushout to remain Boolean is shown to be equivalent to the absence of global sections in the sheaf-theoretic framework of Abramsky and Brandenburger.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a categorical and lattice-theoretic reconstruction of contextuality that precedes probabilistic notions, establishing a precise correspondence between contextuality as a sheaf obstruction and non-distributivity as a colimit failure, clarifying the structural necessity of quantum logic in information-theoretic settings.

title: Geometric Quantum Mechanics in a Symplectic Framework: Metric-Affine Extensions and Deformed Quantum Dynamics
summary:
We present a geometric formulation of quantum mechanics based on the symplectic structure of the projective Hilbert space. Building upon the standard Kähler framework, we introduce an extension in which the symplectic structure is allowed to couple to a metric-affine background geometry, leading to a deformation of the Hamiltonian flow on the state space.
  We show that, under suitable conditions, the deformed structure remains symplectic and defines a well-posed Hamiltonian system. The formulation reduces to standard Schrödinger dynamics in the limit where the geometric deformation vanishes.
  Explicit analytical examples are constructed to illustrate the effect of the deformation. In particular, curvature-dependent deformations lead to a rescaling of Hamiltonian flows, while torsion-induced contributions produce direction-dependent corrections. In addition, geometric phases acquire corrections determined by the deformed symplectic structure.
  These results provide a mathematically consistent framework for exploring geometric modifications of quantum evolution induced by background curvature and affine structure.

AI.tldr: Geometric formulation of quantum mechanics with symplectic structure coupled to metric-affine background geometry, leading to deformed Hamiltonian flow on state space.
AI.motivation: To develop a mathematically consistent framework for exploring geometric modifications of quantum evolution induced by background curvature and affine structure, extending beyond the standard Kähler framework.
AI.method: Extend the standard Kähler framework by allowing the symplectic structure to couple to a metric-affine background geometry, leading to deformation of Hamiltonian flow on the projective Hilbert space state space.
AI.result: The deformed structure remains symplectic under suitable conditions and defines a well-posed Hamiltonian system. Curvature-dependent deformations rescale Hamiltonian flows, torsion-induced contributions produce direction-dependent corrections, and geometric phases acquire corrections from the deformed symplectic structure.
AI.conclusion: The formulation provides a consistent framework for geometric modifications of quantum evolution, reducing to standard Schrödinger dynamics when geometric deformation vanishes, with explicit analytical examples demonstrating curvature and torsion effects.

title: Modeling Quantum Federated Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection in IoT Networks
comment: This paper has been accepted at ICOIN 2026
summary: We propose a Quantum Federated Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection, a framework that leverages quantum federated learning for efficient, secure, and distributed processing in IoT networks. By harnessing quantum autoencoders for high-dimensional feature representation and federated learning for decentralized model training, the approach transforms localized learning on edge devices without requiring transmission of raw data, thereby preserving privacy and minimizing communication overhead. The model leverages quantum advantage in pattern recognition to enhance detection sensitivity, particularly in complex and dynamic IoT network traffic. Experiments on a real-world IoT dataset show that the proposed method delivers anomaly detection accuracy and robustness comparable to centralized approaches, while ensuring data privacy.

AI.tldr: Quantum federated autoencoder framework for IoT anomaly detection that combines quantum computing advantages with federated learning for privacy-preserving distributed processing.
AI.motivation: Need for efficient, secure, and distributed anomaly detection in IoT networks that preserves data privacy while maintaining detection accuracy comparable to centralized approaches.
AI.method: Quantum federated autoencoder framework using quantum autoencoders for high-dimensional feature representation and federated learning for decentralized model training on edge devices without transmitting raw data.
AI.result: Achieves anomaly detection accuracy and robustness comparable to centralized approaches on real-world IoT datasets while ensuring data privacy and minimizing communication overhead.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum federated autoencoder framework successfully enables privacy-preserving, distributed anomaly detection in IoT networks by leveraging quantum advantages in pattern recognition and federated learning principles.

title: Robust Atom Interferometry with Double Bragg Diffraction
comment: PhD thesis, Leibniz University Hannover (2026), xxvi, 146 pages, 54 figures, 4 tables
summary:
This thesis develops a general theoretical and numerical framework for achieving high-contrast atom interferometry based on double Bragg diffraction (DBD). While DBD offers intrinsic symmetry, reduced sensitivity to internal-state systematics, and suitability for microgravity experiments, its performance has long been limited by imperfect diffraction and contrast loss. This work overcomes these limitations by constructing an analytic Hamiltonian description of DBD -- including Doppler effects and polarization imperfections -- and by deriving reduced two- and five-level models via a truncated Magnus-expansion approach. These models clarify the origin of AC-Stark shifts, polarization-induced errors, and Doppler selectivity, and they provide accurate predictions for realistic input momentum distributions.
  Building on this theoretical foundation, the thesis introduces a tri-frequency laser scheme with dynamically tunable detuning and evaluates different detuning-control strategies using a five-level S-matrix formalism. Linear detuning sweeps and optimal-control pulses are shown to provide near-ideal beam-splitter and mirror performance, respectively, ensuring robust contrast across a wide range of experimental imperfections. Complementary full three-dimensional simulations using the GPU-accelerated Universal Atom Interferometer Simulator (UATIS) incorporate interacting Bose-Einstein condensates and realistic optical potentials, revealing transverse effects and polarization-induced distortions that extend the predictions of the one-dimensional non-interacting models. Taken together, this thesis establishes a coherent theoretical and numerical framework demonstrating that, with appropriate detuning control, double-Bragg atom interferometers can achieve the robustness required for precision inertial sensing and future space-based quantum tests of fundamental physics.

AI.tldr: Develops theoretical and numerical framework for high-contrast double Bragg diffraction atom interferometry using analytic Hamiltonian models, tri-frequency laser schemes, and GPU-accelerated simulations to overcome contrast limitations.
AI.motivation: Double Bragg diffraction (DBD) offers intrinsic symmetry, reduced sensitivity to internal-state systematics, and suitability for microgravity experiments, but its performance has been limited by imperfect diffraction and contrast loss. This work aims to overcome these limitations for precision inertial sensing and space-based quantum tests.
AI.method: 1) Constructs analytic Hamiltonian description of DBD including Doppler effects and polarization imperfections; 2) Derives reduced two- and five-level models via truncated Magnus-expansion approach; 3) Introduces tri-frequency laser scheme with dynamically tunable detuning; 4) Evaluates detuning-control strategies using five-level S-matrix formalism; 5) Performs complementary full 3D simulations using GPU-accelerated Universal Atom Interferometer Simulator (UATIS) incorporating interacting Bose-Einstein condensates and realistic optical potentials.
AI.result: Models clarify origin of AC-Stark shifts, polarization-induced errors, and Doppler selectivity, providing accurate predictions for realistic input momentum distributions. Linear detuning sweeps and optimal-control pulses provide near-ideal beam-splitter and mirror performance, ensuring robust contrast across wide range of experimental imperfections. 3D simulations reveal transverse effects and polarization-induced distortions beyond 1D non-interacting models.
AI.conclusion: Establishes coherent theoretical and numerical framework demonstrating that, with appropriate detuning control, double-Bragg atom interferometers can achieve the robustness required for precision inertial sensing and future space-based quantum tests of fundamental physics.

title: Boundary Floquet Control of Bulk non-Hermitian Systems
summary: Non-Hermitian systems provide a powerful platform for engineering and controlling nonequilibrium phenomena beyond Hermitian settings, with the presence of non-Hermitian skin effect broadening the scope of dynamical control. Here, we develop a general theory of non-Hermitian systems driven exclusively at their boundaries, providing a unified description of the driving-frequency dependence of bulk spectra and dynamics in the thermodynamic limit. Our framework extends non-Bloch band theory to time-periodic systems at arbitrary boundary driving frequencies. Applying it to representative models, we demonstrate boundary-driving-induced parity-time symmetry breaking, with the driving frequency serving as a control knob and the driving amplitude providing an additional handle in finite-size systems. These results establish boundary Floquet driving as a versatile mechanism for controlling bulk properties of non-Hermitian systems and open new routes for dynamical engineering in driven open systems.

AI.tldr: General theory for boundary-driven non-Hermitian systems extending non-Bloch band theory to time-periodic systems, enabling control of bulk properties via driving frequency and amplitude.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified framework for understanding and controlling non-Hermitian systems driven exclusively at their boundaries, extending beyond Hermitian settings and leveraging the non-Hermitian skin effect for dynamical control.
AI.method: Developed general theory extending non-Bloch band theory to time-periodic systems with boundary driving. Applied framework to representative models to analyze driving-frequency dependence of bulk spectra and dynamics in thermodynamic limit.
AI.result: Demonstrated boundary-driving-induced parity-time symmetry breaking, with driving frequency serving as control knob and driving amplitude providing additional handle in finite-size systems. Established boundary Floquet driving as versatile mechanism for controlling bulk properties.
AI.conclusion: Boundary Floquet driving provides powerful mechanism for controlling bulk properties of non-Hermitian systems, opening new routes for dynamical engineering in driven open systems beyond Hermitian limitations.

title: Latent Style-based Quantum Wasserstein GAN for Drug Design
comment: Main part: 22 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Supplementary material: 16 pages, 15 figures, 14 tables
summary: The development of new drugs is a tedious, time-consuming, and expensive process, for which the average costs are estimated to be up to around $2.5 billion. The first step in this long process is the design of the new drug, for which de novo drug design, assisted by artificial intelligence, has blossomed in recent years and revolutionized the field. In particular, generative artificial intelligence has delivered promising results in drug discovery and development, reducing costs and the time to solution. However, classical generative models, such as generative adversarial networks (GANs), are difficult to train due to barren plateaus and prone to mode collapse. Quantum computing may be an avenue to overcome these issues and provide models with fewer parameters, thereby enhancing the generalizability of GANs. We propose a new style-based quantum GAN (QGAN) architecture for drug design that implements noise encoding at every rotational gate of the circuit and a gradient penalty in the loss function to mitigate mode collapse. Our pipeline employs a variational autoencoder to represent the molecular structure in a latent space, which is then used as input to our QGAN. Our baseline model runs on up to 15 qubits to validate our architecture on quantum simulators, and a 156-qubit IBM Heron quantum computer in the five-qubit setup is used for inference to investigate the effects of using real quantum hardware on the analysis. We benchmark our results against classical models as provided by the MOSES benchmark suite.

AI.tldr: A quantum style-based GAN architecture for drug design that uses noise encoding and gradient penalty to address classical GAN limitations, validated on quantum simulators and real IBM hardware.
AI.motivation: Drug development is expensive ($2.5B average) and time-consuming. Classical generative models like GANs suffer from training difficulties (barren plateaus, mode collapse). Quantum computing offers potential solutions with fewer parameters and enhanced generalizability for de novo drug design.
AI.method: Proposed style-based quantum GAN architecture with noise encoding at every rotational gate and gradient penalty in loss function to mitigate mode collapse. Pipeline uses variational autoencoder to represent molecular structure in latent space, which feeds into QGAN. Validated on quantum simulators (up to 15 qubits) and IBM Heron quantum computer (5-qubit setup for inference).
AI.result: Architecture validated on quantum simulators and real quantum hardware (IBM Heron). Results benchmarked against classical models using MOSES benchmark suite to evaluate performance improvements.
AI.conclusion: Quantum GANs show promise for overcoming classical GAN limitations in drug design, potentially reducing costs and time in drug discovery through enhanced generalizability and fewer parameters.

title: Probabilistic modeling over permutations using quantum computers
summary: Quantum computers provide a super-exponential speedup for performing a Fourier transform over the symmetric group, an ability for which practical use cases have remained elusive so far. In this work, we leverage this ability to unlock spectral methods for machine learning over permutation-structured data, which appear in applications such as multi-object tracking and recommendation systems. It has been shown previously that a powerful way of building probabilistic models over permutations is to use the framework of non-Abelian harmonic analysis, as the model's group Fourier spectrum captures the interaction complexity: "low frequencies" correspond to low order correlations, and "high frequencies" to more complex ones. This can be used to construct a Markov chain model driven by alternating steps of diffusion (a group-equivariant convolution) and conditioning (a Bayesian update). However, this approach is computationally challenging and hence limited to simple approximations. Here we construct a quantum algorithm that encodes the exact probabilistic model -- a classically intractable object -- into the amplitudes of a quantum state by making use of the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) over the symmetric group. We discuss the scaling, limitations, and practical use of such an approach, which we envision to be a first step towards useful applications of non-Abelian QFTs.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm using symmetric group Fourier transform enables exact probabilistic modeling of permutation-structured data, overcoming classical computational limitations.
AI.motivation: Practical use cases for quantum Fourier transform over symmetric groups have remained elusive, while permutation-structured data appears in important applications like multi-object tracking and recommendation systems where classical spectral methods are computationally limited.
AI.method: Construct quantum algorithm that encodes exact probabilistic model into quantum state amplitudes using Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) over symmetric group, leveraging non-Abelian harmonic analysis framework for permutation modeling.
AI.result: Quantum algorithm enables encoding of classically intractable exact probabilistic models over permutations, with potential for practical applications of non-Abelian QFTs.
AI.conclusion: This represents a first step toward useful applications of non-Abelian QFTs for machine learning over permutation-structured data, overcoming classical computational limitations through quantum advantage.

title: Dicke materials as a resource for quantum squeezing
summary: We study magnetic materials whose low energy physics can be effectively described by a Dicke model, which we term Dicke materials. We show how a Dicke model emerges in such materials due to a coexistence of fast-dispersing and slow-dispersing spins, which are strongly coupled. Analogous to the paradigmatic Dicke model describing light-matter interactions, these materials also exhibit signatures of a superradiant phase transition. The ground state near the superradiant phase transition is expected to be squeezed, making Dicke materials a resource for quantum metrology and witnessing entanglement in solid-state systems. However, as an entanglement measure, squeezing can be sensitive to perturbations that are otherwise irrelevant for usual correlation functions and order parameters. Motivated by the prospect of observing squeezing in such Dicke materials, we study the robustness of ground state squeezing under ubiquitous imperfections such as finite temperature, disorder, and local interactions. Using analytical and numerical techniques, we show that the squeezing obtained is perturbatively stable against these imperfections and quantitatively evaluate regimes promising for experimental observation.

AI.tldr: Dicke materials exhibit superradiant phase transitions with squeezed ground states, which are robust against common imperfections like temperature, disorder, and local interactions, making them promising for quantum metrology and entanglement witnessing.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to explore magnetic materials described by Dicke models that exhibit superradiant phase transitions and squeezed ground states, which could serve as resources for quantum metrology and entanglement witnessing in solid-state systems. The paper aims to study the robustness of this squeezing against practical imperfections to identify experimentally viable regimes.
AI.method: The authors show how Dicke models emerge in magnetic materials through coexistence of fast-dispersing and slow-dispersing strongly coupled spins. They study ground state squeezing near superradiant phase transitions using analytical and numerical techniques to analyze robustness against imperfections like finite temperature, disorder, and local interactions.
AI.result: The squeezing obtained in Dicke materials is perturbatively stable against ubiquitous imperfections including finite temperature, disorder, and local interactions. The authors quantitatively evaluate regimes that are promising for experimental observation of this squeezing.
AI.conclusion: Dicke materials represent a promising platform for quantum metrology and entanglement witnessing due to their robust squeezed ground states near superradiant phase transitions, which remain stable against common experimental imperfections.

title: Preparing Fermions via Classical Sampling and Linear Combinations of Unitaries
summary: We present an extension of the Evolving density matrices on Qubits (E$ρ$OQ) framework that enables efficient fault-tolerant preparation of fermionic quantum states. The original method circumvents state preparation by stochastic sampling, but faces a sign problem in fermionic systems leading to a large number of circuits necessary. We resolve this by combining classical stochastic sampling with a linear combination of unitaries method that avoids the exponential circuit scaling that plagued naïve implementations. The resulting algorithm requires $\mathcal{O}(M^2)$ $R_Z$ rotations for circuit preparation, where $M$ is the number of retained basis states. We validate the method for ground and excited states in the Thirring model, including by computing two-point correlation functions relevant to scattering. In this model for fixed accuracy $\varepsilon$, $M$ is found to scale empirically as $M \propto \frac{1}{mg}\log(1/g)\log(1/m)$.

AI.tldr: Extension of EρOQ framework enables efficient fault-tolerant preparation of fermionic quantum states by combining classical stochastic sampling with linear combination of unitaries to avoid exponential circuit scaling.
AI.motivation: The original EρOQ method circumvents state preparation by stochastic sampling but faces a sign problem in fermionic systems, leading to a large number of circuits necessary for implementation.
AI.method: Combines classical stochastic sampling with a linear combination of unitaries method to avoid exponential circuit scaling that plagued naïve implementations. The algorithm requires O(M²) R_Z rotations for circuit preparation, where M is the number of retained basis states.
AI.result: Validated for ground and excited states in the Thirring model, including computation of two-point correlation functions relevant to scattering. For fixed accuracy ε, M scales empirically as M ∝ (1/mg)log(1/g)log(1/m).
AI.conclusion: The extended EρOQ framework successfully resolves the sign problem in fermionic systems and enables efficient fault-tolerant preparation of fermionic quantum states with polynomial rather than exponential circuit scaling.

title: Predictive supremacy of informationally-restricted quantum perceptron
summary: In the current world, the use of artificial intelligence is penetrating every aspect of human life. The basic element of any artificial intelligence is a digital neuron, called a perceptron, while its quantum analogue is called a quantum perceptron. Here, we introduce a model of perceptron called the informationally-restricted measurement-based perceptron (IMP), where each input is composed of two bits, while at the node, depending on a free input variable, the perceptron decides which bit to evaluate. Additionally, the states transmitted from the input to the node are restricted to a bit (qubit). We establish that under this restriction, the quantum IMP predicts better than a classical IMP. This means that under dimensional restriction of the transmitted states, when both the classical and quantum perceptrons learn the same, the quantum perceptron predicts better than the classical perceptron. For our purpose, we find specific learned values of the perceptron that can display the advantage of a quantum perceptron over its classical counterpart. Restricting to discrete binary inputs, we establish that the observed quantum advantage is universal, that is, for any non-trivial function implementable by both the quantum and classical IMP, one can always find a quantum implementation that outperforms the predictive capability of every classical one. This points to the fact that, given identical learning and resources, a quantum perceptron would predict better than any classical one.

AI.tldr: Quantum perceptrons outperform classical ones under identical learning and resource constraints when information transmission is restricted to single bits/qubits.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate quantum advantage in perceptron models under realistic constraints where information transmission is dimensionally restricted (limited to single bits/qubits), showing that quantum neural networks can outperform classical ones even with identical learning processes.
AI.method: Introduces Informationally-Restricted Measurement-Based Perceptron (IMP) model where inputs are two-bit pairs, the perceptron selects which bit to evaluate based on a free input variable, and transmitted states are restricted to single bits/qubits. Compares quantum vs classical IMP performance under identical learning conditions.
AI.result: Quantum IMP predicts better than classical IMP under dimensional restriction. The quantum advantage is universal for any non-trivial function implementable by both quantum and classical IMP - there always exists a quantum implementation outperforming all classical ones. Given identical learning and resources, quantum perceptrons predict better.
AI.conclusion: Quantum perceptrons demonstrate universal advantage over classical perceptrons under identical learning and resource constraints when information transmission is restricted, suggesting quantum neural networks have superior predictive capabilities even with the same training data and computational resources.

title: Performance of BB84 without decoy states under varying announcement structures
summary: In phase-randomized weak coherent pulse (WCP) implementations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) BB84 protocol, the decoy method is often used to compensate BB84's vulnerability against photon number splitting (PNS) attacks. However, this typically introduces extra complexities and requirements on experimental devices. In this paper, we are therefore interested in phase-randomized WCP implementations without the decoy method. We examine the performance of three QKD protocols with different classical announcement structures, namely BB84, SARG04, and No Public Announcement of Basis (NPAB) BB84, using numerical security proof techniques. We compare secure key rates of the three protocols in asymptotic and finite-size regimes for lossy and noisy channels. The three protocols show different relative advantages depending on the channel behaviour. Canonical BB84 shows robustness against errors and depolarization, SARG04 demonstrates resilience against high loss channels, and NPAB BB84 shows potential advantages against physical misalignment between QKD devices.

AI.tldr: Comparison of three QKD protocols (BB84, SARG04, NPAB BB84) without decoy method in phase-randomized WCP implementations, analyzing their performance under different channel conditions.
AI.motivation: Decoy methods in phase-randomized WCP QKD implementations introduce extra complexities and device requirements; this paper explores alternative approaches without decoy methods to simplify implementations while maintaining security.
AI.method: Numerical security proof techniques applied to compare three QKD protocols with different classical announcement structures: BB84, SARG04, and No Public Announcement of Basis (NPAB) BB84. Analysis conducted in both asymptotic and finite-size regimes for lossy and noisy channels.
AI.result: Different protocols show distinct advantages depending on channel behavior: Canonical BB84 demonstrates robustness against errors and depolarization; SARG04 shows resilience against high loss channels; NPAB BB84 exhibits potential advantages against physical misalignment between QKD devices.
AI.conclusion: Phase-randomized WCP implementations without decoy methods can achieve secure QKD with different protocols offering complementary strengths for various channel conditions, providing simplified alternatives to decoy-based approaches.

title: Geometric Thermodynamics in Open Quantum Systems: Coherence, Curvature, and Work
summary: We formulate a geometric framework for quasistatic thermodynamics in open quantum systems by parameterizing the dynamics on a control manifold. In the quasistatic limit, the system follows a manifold of stationary states, and the work performed over a cycle is given by the flux of a curvature two-form, $W \sim \int Ω$, defined by the parametric response of the stationary state, establishing an open-system analog of classical thermodynamic area laws. For thermal stationary states, the curvature is isotropic and depends only on the instantaneous energy scale, yielding a population-driven geometry in which environmental parameters reshape how work is distributed across the control manifold. Beyond this limit, nonequilibrium stationary states can retain coherence in the energy representation; using a fixed-basis Lindblad model, we show that this coherence reshapes the curvature, making it anisotropic and sign-changing, so that work depends sensitively on the placement and orientation of the cycle. Quantum coherence therefore partitions the control manifold into regions of opposite curvature, producing geometric cancellation of work and allowing the net work over a cycle to be reduced or reversed despite dissipative dynamics. Thermodynamic work thus emerges as a curvature flux whose structure is set by thermodynamic response in classical systems and by basis misalignment between the Hamiltonian eigenbasis and the environment-selected pointer basis in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Geometric framework for quasistatic thermodynamics in open quantum systems shows work over cycles equals flux of curvature two-form, with quantum coherence reshaping curvature and enabling work cancellation/reversal.
AI.motivation: To develop a geometric framework for understanding thermodynamic work in open quantum systems, extending classical thermodynamic area laws to quantum regimes where coherence and environmental interactions play crucial roles.
AI.method: Parameterize dynamics on a control manifold, analyze quasistatic limit where system follows stationary states, compute work as flux of curvature two-form from parametric response, examine thermal vs. nonequilibrium stationary states using fixed-basis Lindblad model.
AI.result: Work over cycle equals flux of curvature two-form; for thermal states curvature is isotropic and population-driven; for coherent nonequilibrium states curvature becomes anisotropic and sign-changing, partitioning control manifold into regions of opposite curvature enabling work cancellation/reversal.
AI.conclusion: Thermodynamic work emerges as curvature flux determined by thermodynamic response in classical systems and by basis misalignment between Hamiltonian eigenbasis and environment-selected pointer basis in open quantum systems, with quantum coherence enabling geometric cancellation effects.

title: Stoquastic permutationally invariant Bell operators
summary: As Hermitian operators, many-body Bell operators can naturally be identified as many-body Hamiltonians. An important subclass of such Hamiltonians is the stoquastic class, characterized by having nonpositive off-diagonal matrix elements in a given basis. Interestingly, this property is shared by the permutationally invariant (PI) Bell operators underlying the largest Bell-correlation experiments to date. In this work, we explore the connection between many-body PI Bell operators and stoquasticity. We introduce the stoquasticity cone, which allows for a full characterization of the stoquastic parameter regimes for any PI Bell operator. We use this to show that PI Bell operators of the binary-input binary-output scenario consisting of at most three-body correlators can always be rendered stoquastic for any set of measurement parameters. Additionally, we also provide examples that use the stoquasticity cone to optimize for the quantum-classical gap. Numerical evidence suggests that the Bell operator used in the largest experiments to date is optimal with respect to stoquasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this work establishes the first connection between PI Bell operators and stoquasticity.

AI.tldr: PI Bell operators can be viewed as Hamiltonians, and their stoquasticity (nonpositive off-diagonal elements) is analyzed via a stoquasticity cone, showing that certain classes can always be made stoquastic and providing optimization tools.
AI.motivation: To explore the connection between permutationally invariant (PI) Bell operators and stoquastic Hamiltonians, since PI Bell operators from largest Bell-correlation experiments share the stoquastic property of having nonpositive off-diagonal matrix elements.
AI.method: Introduce the stoquasticity cone to characterize stoquastic parameter regimes for any PI Bell operator. Analyze binary-input binary-output PI Bell operators with up to three-body correlators, and use the cone to optimize quantum-classical gaps.
AI.result: PI Bell operators with binary-input binary-output and at most three-body correlators can always be rendered stoquastic for any measurement parameters. Numerical evidence suggests the Bell operator used in largest experiments is optimal with respect to stoquasticity.
AI.conclusion: Establishes first connection between PI Bell operators and stoquasticity, providing tools to characterize and optimize stoquastic regimes, with implications for understanding Bell correlation experiments through Hamiltonian properties.

title: Distance-Finding Algorithms for Quantum Codes and Circuits
summary: The distance of a classical or quantum code is a key figure of merit which reflects its capacity to detect errors. Quantum LDPC code families have considerable promise in reducing the overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but calculating their distance is challenging with existing methods. We generally assess the performance of a quantum code under circuit level error models, and for such scenarios the circuit distance is an important consideration. Calculating circuit distance is in general more difficult than finding the distance of the corresponding code as the detector error matrix of the circuit is usually much larger than the code's check matrix. In this work, we benchmark a wide range of distance-finding methods for various classical and quantum code families, as well as syndrome-extraction circuits. We consider both exact methods (such as Brouwer-Zimmermann, connected cluster, SAT and mixed integer programming) and heuristic methods which have lower run-time but can only give a bound on distance (examples include random information set, syndrome decoder algorithms, and Stim undetectable error methods). We further develop the QDistEvol algorithm and show that it performs well for the quantum LDPC codes in our benchmark. The algorithms and test data have been made available to the community in the codeDistance Python package.

AI.tldr: Benchmarking study comparing various distance-finding methods for classical/quantum codes and syndrome-extraction circuits, with development of QDistEvol algorithm for quantum LDPC codes.
AI.motivation: Distance calculation is crucial for assessing code performance but challenging, especially for quantum LDPC codes and circuit distance which is more difficult than code distance calculation.
AI.method: Benchmark multiple distance-finding methods including exact (Brouwer-Zimmermann, connected cluster, SAT, mixed integer programming) and heuristic approaches (random information set, syndrome decoder, Stim undetectable error). Develop QDistEvol algorithm specifically for quantum LDPC codes.
AI.result: QDistEvol algorithm performs well for quantum LDPC codes in benchmark. All algorithms and test data made available in codeDistance Python package.
AI.conclusion: Comprehensive benchmarking provides practical tools for distance calculation, with QDistEvol showing promise for quantum LDPC codes, addressing a key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Development of Biphoton Entangled Light Spectroscopy (BELS) using Bell pairs
summary: We introduce Biphoton Entanglement Light Spectroscopy (BELS), a quantum spectroscopic technique that employs polarization entangled Bell pairs and two photon interference to probe material properties. In BELS, the measured signal arises not from single photon intensities but from changes in the joint polarization and path correlations of biphoton Bell pairs transmitted through or scattered by a sample and analyzed via cross channel coincidences. A key concept of BELS is the explicit mapping between Jones matrix operations and transformations within the Bell state manifold. Optical elements that are equivalent under classical polarization optics can produce qualitatively distinct signatures in the coincidence landscape when interrogated with entangled photons. We demonstrate that linear birefringence and Faraday rotation generate orthogonal admixtures of Bell states, yielding experimentally distinguishable coincidence channels within a single measurement. We measure birefringence in an anisotropic dielectric and Faraday rotation in $\text{Tb}_3\text{Ga}_5\text{O}_{12}$. By mapping the changes to the photonic entanglement, BELS establishes a new framework for future entanglement enhanced spectroscopy, a potentially powerful approach in characterizing quantum materials, nanophotonic devices, and light matter interactions perhaps eventually at a fundamentally quantum level.

AI.tldr: BELS is a quantum spectroscopy technique using polarization-entangled photon pairs and two-photon interference to probe materials, mapping Jones matrix operations to Bell state transformations for enhanced sensitivity.
AI.motivation: To develop a new spectroscopic approach that leverages quantum entanglement to probe material properties beyond classical limits, potentially enabling more sensitive characterization of quantum materials, nanophotonic devices, and light-matter interactions.
AI.method: Uses polarization-entangled Bell pairs and two-photon interference; measures changes in joint polarization and path correlations of biphotons transmitted/scattered through samples via cross-channel coincidences; maps Jones matrix operations to transformations within Bell state manifold.
AI.result: Demonstrated that linear birefringence and Faraday rotation generate orthogonal Bell state admixtures with distinguishable coincidence channels; measured birefringence in anisotropic dielectric and Faraday rotation in Tb₃Ga₅O₁₂; established mapping between optical operations and entanglement transformations.
AI.conclusion: BELS establishes a new framework for entanglement-enhanced spectroscopy with potential applications in characterizing quantum materials, nanophotonic devices, and fundamental light-matter interactions at the quantum level.

title: Effect of the Atomic Dipole-Dipole Interaction on the Phase Diagrams of Field-Matter Interactions
summary: Quantum information measures are used to study the quantum phase diagrams of the two-level Dicke model including the atomic dipole-dipole interaction, for a finite number of particles, with and without the rotating-wave approximation, which yields the conservation of the total number of excitations in the first case and its parity in the general case. We show that the quantum phase transitions can be observed in the fluctuation of the atomic populations and that of the number of photons, and also that the conditional probability distribution of the population of the excited state with zero photons carries the information of the quantum phase transitions when the matter-field interaction is weak.

AI.tldr: Quantum phase transitions in the two-level Dicke model with atomic dipole-dipole interactions can be detected through fluctuations in atomic populations and photon numbers, and via conditional probability distributions of excited state populations with zero photons in weak coupling regimes.
AI.motivation: To investigate quantum phase diagrams of the two-level Dicke model with atomic dipole-dipole interactions for finite particle numbers, analyzing both rotating-wave approximation (RWA) and non-RWA cases, and to identify observable signatures of quantum phase transitions in measurable quantities.
AI.method: Utilizes quantum information measures to study the two-level Dicke model with atomic dipole-dipole interactions. Analyzes both cases: with rotating-wave approximation (conserving total excitations) and without RWA (conserving excitation parity). Examines fluctuations in atomic populations and photon numbers, and conditional probability distributions of excited state populations with zero photons.
AI.result: Quantum phase transitions can be observed through fluctuations in atomic populations and photon numbers. Additionally, the conditional probability distribution of the excited state population with zero photons carries information about quantum phase transitions when the matter-field interaction is weak.
AI.conclusion: Quantum information measures provide effective tools for detecting quantum phase transitions in the Dicke model with dipole-dipole interactions, with specific observables (population fluctuations and conditional probability distributions) serving as signatures of these transitions, particularly in weak coupling regimes.

title: Deterministic quantum master equation for non-Markovian signal processing
summary: In this work, we derive a deterministic master equation to model a general, possibly non-Markovian, feedback. The master equation describes a system with a general evolution and measurement operation, with feedback being applied in terms of signal processing. The feedback signal has an arbitrary structure with dimensionality that indicates the degree of non-Markovianity of the information processing. We present examples to illustrate how such a master equation can be used to model systems with memory feedback and non-trivial frequency dependence.

AI.tldr: Derivation of deterministic master equation for general non-Markovian feedback systems with arbitrary signal structure and dimensionality indicating degree of non-Markovianity.
AI.motivation: To develop a comprehensive framework for modeling general feedback systems, including non-Markovian cases, where feedback signals have complex temporal structure and memory effects.
AI.method: Derivation of deterministic master equation describing systems with general evolution and measurement operations, with feedback implemented through signal processing. The feedback signal has arbitrary structure with dimensionality indicating non-Markovianity degree.
AI.result: A master equation framework capable of modeling systems with memory feedback and non-trivial frequency dependence, demonstrated through illustrative examples.
AI.conclusion: The derived master equation provides a versatile tool for analyzing general feedback systems, particularly those with non-Markovian characteristics and complex signal processing requirements.

title: Optimal filtering for a giant cavity in waveguide QED systems
summary: In waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED) systems, a giant cavity can be engineered to interact with quantum fields by multiple distant coupling points so that its non-Markovian dynamics are quite different from traditional quantum optical cavity systems. Towards feedback control this system, this paper designs an optimal filter for the giant cavity systems to estimate its state evolution under continuous quantum measurements. Firstly, the Langevin equation in the Heisenberg picture are derived, which is a linear continuous-time system with both states and inputs delays resulting from the unconventional distant couplings. Compared to existing modeling approaches, this formulation effectively preserves the nonlocal coupling and multiple delay dynamic characteristics inherent in the original system. In particular, the presence of coupling and propagation delays leads to noncommutativity among the system operators at different times, which prevents the direct application of existing quantum filtering methods. To address this issue, an optimal filter is designed, in which the delayed-state covariance matrices are computed. By iteratively evaluating the delayed-state covariance over successive time intervals, the resulting optimal filter can be implemented in an interval-wise backward recursion algorithm. Finally, numerical simulations are conducted to evaluate the tracking performance of the proposed optimal filter for the giant cavity. By comparing between the evolutions of Wigner functions of coherent and cat states and the filter, the effectiveness of the optimal filter is validated.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an optimal quantum filter for giant cavity waveguide QED systems with multiple distant coupling points, addressing the challenges of non-Markovian dynamics and time delays in state estimation under continuous measurements.
AI.motivation: Giant cavity waveguide QED systems exhibit unique non-Markovian dynamics due to multiple distant coupling points, creating challenges for state estimation that cannot be addressed by traditional quantum filtering methods designed for Markovian systems.
AI.method: The authors derive Langevin equations in the Heisenberg picture to model the system as a linear continuous-time system with state and input delays. They design an optimal filter by computing delayed-state covariance matrices and implementing an interval-wise backward recursion algorithm to handle noncommutativity issues arising from coupling and propagation delays.
AI.result: Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed optimal filter effectively tracks the state evolution of giant cavity systems, as validated by comparing Wigner function evolutions of coherent and cat states between the actual system and the filter.
AI.conclusion: The developed optimal filter successfully addresses the challenges of non-Markovian dynamics and time delays in giant cavity waveguide QED systems, enabling accurate state estimation under continuous quantum measurements for feedback control applications.

title: Sub-nanometer resolution of the nitrogen-vacancy center by Fourier magnetic imaging
summary: Solid-state spins in diamond are promising building blocks for quantum computing and quantum sensing, both of which require precise nanoscale addressing of individual spins. To explore the resolution limit of this approach, we demonstrate Fourier magnetic imaging of nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond under state-of-the-art conditions. We constructed a highly compact experimental platform featuring thermal drift compensation under ambient conditions and generated a pulsed magnetic field gradient of up to 13.5 G/$μ$m. By implementing the Fourier magnetic imaging protocol, we achieved localization of a single nitrogen-vacancy center with a spatial resolution of 0.28 $\pm$ 0.10 nm and a magnetic field measurement deviation of 9 nT. This technique holds potential for applications such as localizing spins within proteins and cells.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of Fourier magnetic imaging achieving 0.28 nm spatial resolution for single nitrogen-vacancy center localization in diamond using pulsed magnetic field gradients up to 13.5 G/μm.
AI.motivation: Solid-state spins in diamond are promising for quantum computing and sensing, requiring precise nanoscale addressing of individual spins. The research aims to explore the resolution limits of magnetic imaging techniques for nitrogen-vacancy centers.
AI.method: Constructed a highly compact experimental platform with thermal drift compensation under ambient conditions, generated pulsed magnetic field gradients up to 13.5 G/μm, and implemented Fourier magnetic imaging protocol for nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond.
AI.result: Achieved localization of a single nitrogen-vacancy center with spatial resolution of 0.28 ± 0.10 nm and magnetic field measurement deviation of 9 nT, representing state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: The Fourier magnetic imaging technique demonstrates exceptional nanoscale resolution for spin localization, with potential applications in localizing spins within proteins and cells for biological and quantum sensing applications.

title: Interference-induced state engineering and Hamiltonian control for noisy collective-spin metrology
summary: Interference provides a fundamental mechanism for generating and manipulating entanglement in many-body quantum systems. Here, we develop an interference framework in which the nonlinear dynamics of collective spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ ensembles are mapped onto phase accumulation and self-interference in phase space, providing a direct and physically transparent description of entanglement formation. Within this framework, one-axis twisting produces Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, while two-axis twisting generates multi-component GHZ superpositions relevant for multiparameter quantum metrology. Building on this interference-based description, we analyze metrological performance under realistic Markovian noise, including local and collective emission, pumping, and dephasing, and examine the role of Hamiltonian control based on linear and nonlinear interactions. We show that while control can enhance single-parameter sensitivity in a noise-dependent regime, the achievable precision in multiparameter estimation is fundamentally constrained. These results establish interference as a unifying principle linking nonlinear dynamics, entanglement generation, and metrological performance, and reveal intrinsic limitations of multiparameter quantum sensing. Our framework provides broadly applicable insight into the design of robust quantum-enhanced measurement protocols in noisy many-body systems.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an interference framework mapping collective spin dynamics to phase space interference, revealing how entanglement forms and analyzing metrological performance under noise with fundamental multiparameter limitations.
AI.motivation: To establish interference as a unifying principle linking nonlinear dynamics, entanglement generation, and metrological performance in many-body quantum systems, providing physically transparent descriptions of entanglement formation and analyzing realistic noise effects.
AI.method: Develops an interference framework mapping nonlinear dynamics of collective spin-1/2 ensembles onto phase accumulation and self-interference in phase space. Analyzes metrological performance under Markovian noise (local/collective emission, pumping, dephasing) and examines Hamiltonian control using linear and nonlinear interactions.
AI.result: One-axis twisting produces GHZ states, two-axis twisting generates multi-component GHZ superpositions for multiparameter metrology. Control enhances single-parameter sensitivity in noise-dependent regimes, but multiparameter estimation precision is fundamentally constrained. Interference framework provides direct description of entanglement formation.
AI.conclusion: Interference serves as a unifying principle connecting nonlinear dynamics, entanglement generation, and metrological performance, revealing intrinsic limitations of multiparameter quantum sensing. The framework provides broadly applicable insight for designing robust quantum-enhanced measurement protocols in noisy many-body systems.

title: Boundary-sensitive non-Hermiticity of Floquet Hamiltonian: spectral transition and scale-free localization
summary: We report a novel mechanism of boundary-sensitive PT symmetry breaking in one-dimensional Floquet systems. By designing a time-periodic driving protocol, we realize a Floquet Hamiltonian that is Hermitian under periodic boundary conditions yet acquires non-Hermitian boundary terms under open boundary conditions due to the non-commutativity of driving Hamiltonians. We establish that a PT symmetry breaking transition occurs when the quasienergy bandwidth expands to cover the entire frequency Brillouin zone. This condition highlights a crucial difference from static non-Hermitian systems, where such transitions typically require band touching. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in the PT-broken phase, the eigenstates exhibit scale-free localization, a phenomenon arising from the specific system-size scaling of non-Hermitian terms. Finally, we provide a general framework for constructing multi-band models that exhibit this boundary-induced phase transition.

AI.tldr: Boundary-sensitive PT symmetry breaking in 1D Floquet systems through time-periodic driving, where Hermitian periodic boundary conditions become non-Hermitian under open boundaries, leading to PT breaking when quasienergy bandwidth covers the full frequency Brillouin zone.
AI.motivation: To discover a novel mechanism of PT symmetry breaking that is sensitive to boundary conditions in Floquet systems, distinguishing it from static non-Hermitian systems where such transitions typically require band touching.
AI.method: Design time-periodic driving protocols to realize Floquet Hamiltonians that are Hermitian under periodic boundary conditions but acquire non-Hermitian boundary terms under open boundary conditions due to non-commutativity of driving Hamiltonians.
AI.result: PT symmetry breaking occurs when quasienergy bandwidth expands to cover the entire frequency Brillouin zone; in the PT-broken phase, eigenstates exhibit scale-free localization due to system-size scaling of non-Hermitian terms.
AI.conclusion: Established a boundary-sensitive PT symmetry breaking mechanism unique to Floquet systems and provided a general framework for constructing multi-band models exhibiting this boundary-induced phase transition.

title: Charging efficiency bursts in a quantum battery with cyclic indefinite causal order
summary: Enhancement of quantum battery performance is a popular subject in quantum thermodynamics. An interesting phenomenon is the quick charging effect [Phys. Rev. Res. 6, 023136 (2024)], which has been explored by utilizing a quantum interferometric technique known as superposition of trajectories. A similar technique used to boost quantum battery performance is indefinite causal order. Here, we propose a new charging protocol that utilizes cyclic indefinite causal order, whereby $N$ charging sequences are superposed when utilizing $N$ chargers. We observe charging efficiency bursts when implementing our cyclic indefinite charging protocol. The duration of these bursts increase with $N$. Additionally, we present a circuit model to implement our charging protocol for the two-charger scenario and perform proof-of-concept demonstrations on IonQ, Quantinuum and IBMQ quantum processors. The results validate the existence of charging efficiency bursts as shown by our theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: A new quantum battery charging protocol using cyclic indefinite causal order shows efficiency bursts that increase with number of chargers, validated experimentally on quantum processors.
AI.motivation: To enhance quantum battery performance by developing a novel charging protocol that goes beyond existing techniques like superposition of trajectories and indefinite causal order.
AI.method: Proposed cyclic indefinite causal order protocol where N charging sequences are superposed using N chargers, with circuit model implementation for two-charger scenario and experimental demonstrations on IonQ, Quantinuum and IBMQ quantum processors.
AI.result: Observed charging efficiency bursts whose duration increases with N, with experimental results validating theoretical predictions and numerical simulations.
AI.conclusion: Cyclic indefinite causal order provides an effective method for quantum battery charging with efficiency bursts, experimentally demonstrated on current quantum hardware.

title: Enabling Chemically Accurate Quantum Phase Estimation in the Early Fault-Tolerant Regime
summary: Quantum simulation of molecular electronic structure is one of the most promising applications of quantum computing. However, achieving chemically accurate predictions for strongly correlated systems requires quantum phase estimation (QPE) on fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) devices. Existing resource estimates for typical FTQC architectures suggest that such calculations demand millions of physical qubits, thereby placing them beyond the reach of near-term devices. Here, we investigate the feasibility of performing QPE for chemically relevant molecular systems in an early-FTQC regime, characterized by partial fault tolerance, constrained qubit budgets, and limited circuit depth. Our framework is based on single-ancilla, Trotter-based QPE implementations combined with partially randomized time evolution. Within this framework, we develop a novel Hamiltonian optimization strategy, termed unitary weight concentration, that reduces algorithmic cost by reshaping linear-combination-of-unitaries representations. Applying this framework to active-space models of iron-sulfur clusters, cytochrome P450 active sites, and CO$_2$-utilization catalysts, we perform end-to-end resource estimation using the latest version of the space-time efficient analog rotation (STAR) architecture. Our results indicate that ground-state energy estimation for active spaces of approximately 20 to 50 spatial orbitals, well beyond the reach of classical full configuration interaction, is achievable using $\sim 10^5$ physical qubits, with runtimes on the order of days to weeks. These findings demonstrate that while full-fledged fault-tolerant quantum computers will be required for even larger molecular simulations, chemically meaningful quantum chemistry problems are already within reach in an experimentally relevant, early-FTQC regime.

AI.tldr: Quantum phase estimation for molecular systems is feasible in early fault-tolerant quantum computing regime with ~10^5 physical qubits, enabling chemically accurate simulations for 20-50 orbital active spaces beyond classical capabilities.
AI.motivation: Current fault-tolerant quantum computing resource estimates require millions of physical qubits for quantum phase estimation of strongly correlated molecular systems, placing such calculations beyond near-term capabilities. The paper aims to explore whether chemically relevant quantum chemistry problems can be addressed in an early-FTQC regime with partial fault tolerance, constrained qubit budgets, and limited circuit depth.
AI.method: Developed a framework combining single-ancilla, Trotter-based quantum phase estimation with partially randomized time evolution. Introduced a novel Hamiltonian optimization strategy called "unitary weight concentration" that reduces algorithmic cost by reshaping linear-combination-of-unitaries representations. Applied this framework to active-space models of iron-sulfur clusters, cytochrome P450 active sites, and CO₂-utilization catalysts, performing end-to-end resource estimation using the space-time efficient analog rotation (STAR) architecture.
AI.result: Ground-state energy estimation for active spaces of approximately 20 to 50 spatial orbitals (beyond classical full configuration interaction capabilities) is achievable using ~10^5 physical qubits, with runtimes on the order of days to weeks. This represents a significant reduction from previous estimates requiring millions of qubits.
AI.conclusion: While full fault-tolerant quantum computers will be needed for larger molecular simulations, chemically meaningful quantum chemistry problems are already within reach in an experimentally relevant early-FTQC regime. The proposed framework and optimization strategies enable practical quantum simulations of strongly correlated molecular systems with substantially reduced resource requirements.

title: Understanding Bugs in Quantum Simulators: An Empirical Study
summary:
Quantum simulators are a foundational component of the quantum software ecosystem. They are widely used to develop and debug quantum programs, validate compiler transformations, and support empirical claims about correctness and performance. In the absence of large-scale quantum hardware, simulator outputs are often treated as ground truth for algorithm development and system evaluation. However, quantum simulators also introduce unique implementation challenges. They must faithfully emulate quantum behavior while executing on classical hardware, requiring complex representations of quantum state evolution, operator composition, and noise modeling. Yet, we still lack a large-scale and in-depth study of failures in quantum simulators.
  To bridge this gap, this work presents a comprehensive empirical study of bugs in widely used open-source quantum simulators. We analyze 394 confirmed bugs from 12 simulators and manually categorize them based on root causes, failure manifestations, affected components, and discovery mechanisms. Our study reveals several key findings. First, bug discovery is largely user-driven, with most crashes, exceptions, and resource-related failures not detected by automated testing and identified after deployment. Second, logical correctness failures are widespread and often silent, producing plausible but incorrect outputs without triggering crashes or explicit error signals. Third, many critical failures originate in classical simulator infrastructure, such as memory management, indexing, configuration, and dependency compatibility, rather than in core quantum execution logic. These findings provide new insights into the reliability challenges of quantum simulators and highlight opportunities to improve testing and validation practices in the quantum software ecosystem.

AI.tldr: Comprehensive empirical study of 394 bugs in 12 open-source quantum simulators reveals user-driven discovery, widespread silent logical correctness failures, and critical infrastructure issues.
AI.motivation: Quantum simulators are foundational to quantum software development but face unique implementation challenges. Despite being treated as ground truth, there's a lack of large-scale studies on simulator failures, creating a gap in understanding their reliability challenges.
AI.method: Empirical analysis of 394 confirmed bugs from 12 widely used open-source quantum simulators, with manual categorization based on root causes, failure manifestations, affected components, and discovery mechanisms.
AI.result: Three key findings: 1) Bug discovery is largely user-driven with most failures not caught by automated testing; 2) Logical correctness failures are widespread and often silent, producing plausible but incorrect outputs; 3) Critical failures often originate in classical simulator infrastructure rather than core quantum execution logic.
AI.conclusion: The study provides new insights into quantum simulator reliability challenges and highlights opportunities to improve testing and validation practices in the quantum software ecosystem.

title: Quantum Random Forest for the Regression Problem
comment: Accepted in Quantum Computing - Artificial Intelligence for Industry Applications and Scientific Discovery A Workshop at the IEEE International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC) 2026
summary: The Random Forest model is one of the popular models of Machine learning. We present a quantum algorithm for testing (forecasting) process of the Random Forest machine learning model for the Regression problem. The presented algorithm is more efficient (in terms of query complexity or running time) than the classical counterpart.

AI.tldr: Quantum algorithm for Random Forest regression testing that outperforms classical methods in query complexity and runtime.
AI.motivation: Random Forest is a popular ML model, and quantum computing offers potential efficiency gains for forecasting tasks in regression problems.
AI.method: Developed a quantum algorithm specifically designed for testing/forecasting with Random Forest models for regression problems.
AI.result: The quantum algorithm demonstrates superior efficiency compared to classical counterparts in terms of query complexity and running time.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing can provide significant performance advantages for Random Forest regression testing, offering more efficient forecasting capabilities.

title: Exponential Separation of Quantum and Classical One-Way Numbers-on-Forehead Communication
summary:
Numbers-on-Forehead (NOF) communication model is a central model in communication complexity. As a restricted variant, one-way NOF model is of particular interest. Establishing strong one-way NOF lower bounds would imply circuit lower bounds, resolve well-known problems in additive combinatorics, and yield wide-ranging applications in areas such as cryptography and distributed computing. However, proving strong lower bounds in one-way NOF communication remains highly challenging; many fundamental questions in one-way NOF communication remain wide open. One of the fundamental questions, proposed by Gavinsky and Pudlák (CCC 2008), is to establish an explicit exponential separation between quantum and classical one-way NOF communication.
  In this paper, we resolve this open problem by establishing the first exponential separation between quantum and randomized communication complexity in one-way NOF model. Specifically, we define a lifted variant of the Hidden Matching problem of Bar-Yossef, Jayram, and Kerenidis (STOC 2004) and show that it admits an ($O(\log n)$)-cost quantum protocol in the one-way NOF setting. By contrast, we prove that any $k$-party one-way randomized protocol for this problem requires communication $Ω(\frac{n^{1/3}}{2^{k/3}})$. Notably, our separation applies even to a generalization of $k$-player one-way communication, where the first player speaks once, and all other $k-1$ players can communicate freely.

AI.tldr: First exponential separation between quantum and classical one-way NOF communication complexity via lifted Hidden Matching problem.
AI.motivation: Resolve Gavinsky and Pudlák's 2008 open problem about explicit exponential separation between quantum and classical one-way NOF communication, which has implications for circuit lower bounds, additive combinatorics, cryptography, and distributed computing.
