AI.method: Define a lifted variant of the Hidden Matching problem and analyze its communication complexity: construct O(log n)-cost quantum protocol in one-way NOF setting, and prove Ω(n^{1/3}/2^{k/3}) lower bound for any k-party one-way randomized protocol.
AI.result: Achieve exponential separation: quantum protocol costs O(log n) while randomized protocols require Ω(n^{1/3}/2^{k/3}) communication, establishing first explicit exponential gap between quantum and classical one-way NOF communication.
AI.conclusion: Resolve long-standing open problem by demonstrating exponential quantum advantage in one-way NOF communication model, with separation applying even to generalized communication setting where first player speaks once and others communicate freely.

title: Encoded Quantum Signal Processing for Heisenberg-Limited Metrology
summary: Entangled quantum probes can achieve Heisenberg-limited measurement precision, but this advantage is typically destroyed by noise. We address this issue by introducing a framework that we call encoded quantum signal processing, which unifies quantum error detection and quantum signal processing into an effective single-qubit framework, and provides a paradigm for constructing logical sensors that are robust to noise while remaining sensitive to the signal of interest. We show that encoding sensor qubits into a repetition code and using syndrome measurements as a signal-processing primitive restores Heisenberg scaling under realistic noise, without applying recovery operations. We prove that product-state sensing with syndrome post-processing is fundamentally limited to standard quantum limit (SQL) scaling, and develop four protocols that overcome this barrier through entanglement or sequential signal amplification, achieving Heisenberg-limited precision with exponential error suppression in code distance. For spatially inhomogeneous fields, Bayesian marginalization preserves Heisenberg scaling provided noise decreases sufficiently with system size. The underlying mechanism, which we formalize as encoded quantum signal processing, reduces multi-qubit metrology to an effective single-qubit problem where syndrome measurement implements nonlinear signal transformations. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical predictions: syndrome-based inference achieves near-Heisenberg scaling at noise levels where bare probes approach the SQL, and a concatenated protocol maintains this scaling under joint transverse noise and longitudinal inhomogeneities.

AI.tldr: Framework called "encoded quantum signal processing" unifies quantum error detection and signal processing to create logical sensors that achieve Heisenberg-limited precision under realistic noise without recovery operations.
AI.motivation: Entangled quantum probes can achieve Heisenberg-limited measurement precision, but this advantage is typically destroyed by noise. There's a need for quantum sensing protocols that maintain Heisenberg scaling under realistic noise conditions.
AI.method: Introduces encoded quantum signal processing framework that unifies quantum error detection and quantum signal processing. Uses repetition code encoding of sensor qubits with syndrome measurements as signal-processing primitive. Develops four protocols using entanglement or sequential signal amplification. For spatially inhomogeneous fields, uses Bayesian marginalization.
AI.result: Encoding sensor qubits into repetition code with syndrome measurements restores Heisenberg scaling under realistic noise without recovery operations. Product-state sensing with syndrome post-processing is fundamentally limited to SQL scaling, but developed protocols overcome this barrier. Numerical simulations validate theoretical predictions: syndrome-based inference achieves near-Heisenberg scaling at noise levels where bare probes approach SQL, and concatenated protocol maintains scaling under joint transverse noise and longitudinal inhomogeneities.
AI.conclusion: Encoded quantum signal processing provides a paradigm for constructing logical sensors robust to noise while remaining sensitive to signals of interest. The framework reduces multi-qubit metrology to an effective single-qubit problem where syndrome measurement implements nonlinear signal transformations, enabling Heisenberg-limited precision with exponential error suppression in code distance.

title: RC-HEOM Hybrid Method for Non-Perturbative Open System Dynamics
comment: 7 page, 3 figure, 2 tables in main tex. 7 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables in supplemental material
summary: The Hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) method is an important non-perturbative technique, allowing numerically exact treatment of open quantum systems with strong coupling and non-Markovian memory. However, its encoding of bath memory into auxiliary density operators often limits direct access to detailed bath information. In contrast, the reaction-coordinate (RC) mapping allows direct and transparent access to the dominant collective bath mode, but its perturbative and often Markovian treatment of the residual bath restricts its reliability. In this work, we introduce RC-HEOM, a hybrid method that unifies the strengths of both approaches by combining RC mapping with a fully non-perturbative HEOM description of the residual bath. RC-HEOM simultaneously retains exact non-Markovian memory and access to the RC mode, which enables analysis of system-RC information. Applying this method to the Anderson impurity models, we directly track the emergence of the Kondo singlet from the growth of the Kondo resonance and uncover a nontrivial RC-mediated coherence revival. These results demonstrate that RC-HEOM is a promising method for characterizing open quantum systems in regimes that are difficult to access with conventional master-equation methods.

AI.tldr: RC-HEOM hybrid method combines reaction-coordinate mapping with hierarchical equations of motion to enable exact non-Markovian treatment while providing direct access to collective bath mode information.
AI.motivation: HEOM provides exact non-Markovian treatment but lacks direct bath information access, while RC mapping offers transparent access to collective bath modes but relies on perturbative Markovian approximations. A unified approach is needed to combine both strengths.
AI.method: RC-HEOM hybrid method that first applies reaction-coordinate mapping to extract dominant collective bath mode, then treats the residual bath non-perturbatively using hierarchical equations of motion, enabling exact non-Markovian treatment with direct access to RC mode information.
AI.result: Applied to Anderson impurity models, the method directly tracks Kondo singlet emergence from Kondo resonance growth and reveals nontrivial RC-mediated coherence revival, demonstrating capabilities beyond conventional master-equation methods.
AI.conclusion: RC-HEOM is a promising unified method for characterizing open quantum systems in regimes difficult to access with conventional approaches, combining exact non-Markovian memory with direct access to collective bath mode information.

title: STAR-Magic Mutation: Even More Efficient Analog Rotation Gates for Early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computer
summary: We introduce STAR-magic mutation, an efficient protocol for implementing logical rotation gates on early fault-tolerant quantum computers. This protocol judiciously combines two of the latest state preparation protocols: transversal multi-rotation protocol and magic state cultivation. It achieves a logical rotation gate with a favorable error scaling of $\mathcal{O}(θ_L^{2(1-Θ(1/d))}p_{\text{ph}})$, while requiring only the ancillary space of a single surface code patch. Here, $θ_L$ is the logical rotation angle, $p_{\text{ph}}$ is the physical error rate, and $d$ is the code distance. This scaling marks a significant improvement over the previous state-of-the-art, $\mathcal{O}(θ_L p_{\text{ph}})$, making our protocol particularly powerful for implementing a sequence of small-angle rotation gates, like Trotter-based circuits. Notably, for $θ_L \lesssim 10^{-5}$, our protocol achieves a two-order-of-magnitude reduction in both the execution time and the error rate of analog rotation gates compared to the standard $T$-gate synthesis using cultivated magic states. Building upon this protocol, we also propose a novel quantum computing architecture designed for early fault-tolerant quantum computers, dubbed ``STAR ver.~3". It employs a refined circuit compilation strategy based on Clifford+$T$+$φ$ gate set, rather than the conventional Clifford+$T$ or Clifford+$φ$ gate sets. We establish a theoretical bound on the feasible circuit size on this architecture and illustrate its capabilities by analyzing the spacetime costs for simulating the dynamics of quantum many-body systems. Specifically, we demonstrate that our architecture can simulate biologically-relevant molecules or lattice models at scales beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, with only a few hundred thousand physical qubits, even assuming a realistic error rate of $p_{\text{ph}}=10^{-3}$.

AI.tldr: STAR-magic mutation protocol combines transversal multi-rotation and magic state cultivation to implement logical rotation gates with improved error scaling O(θ_L^{2(1-Θ(1/d))}p_ph), requiring only single surface code patch ancillary space.
AI.motivation: To develop efficient protocols for implementing logical rotation gates on early fault-tolerant quantum computers, addressing the limitations of previous methods with O(θ_L p_ph) scaling, particularly for small-angle rotations in Trotter-based circuits.
AI.method: Combines transversal multi-rotation protocol and magic state cultivation to create STAR-magic mutation protocol. Also proposes STAR ver. 3 architecture using Clifford+T+φ gate set compilation rather than conventional Clifford+T or Clifford+φ sets.
AI.result: Achieves two-order-of-magnitude reduction in execution time and error rate for θ_L ≲ 10^{-5} compared to standard T-gate synthesis with cultivated magic states. Theoretical bound on feasible circuit size established. Architecture can simulate biologically-relevant molecules/lattice models beyond classical reach with few hundred thousand physical qubits at p_ph=10^{-3} error rate.
AI.conclusion: STAR-magic mutation protocol provides significant improvement in error scaling for logical rotation gates, enabling more efficient implementation of small-angle rotations. The proposed STAR ver. 3 architecture with refined compilation strategy offers practical path for early fault-tolerant quantum computing applications.

title: A PAC-Bayesian approach to generalization for quantum models
summary: Generalization is a central concept in machine learning theory, yet for quantum models, it is predominantly analyzed through uniform bounds that depend on a model's overall capacity rather than the specific function learned. These capacity-based uniform bounds are often too loose and entirely insensitive to the actual training and learning process. Previous theoretical guarantees have failed to provide non-uniform, data-dependent bounds that reflect the specific properties of the learned solution rather than the worst-case behavior of the entire hypothesis class. To address this limitation, we derive the first PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for a broad class of quantum models by analyzing layered circuits composed of general quantum channels, which include dissipative operations such as mid-circuit measurements and feedforward. Through a channel perturbation analysis, we establish non-uniform bounds that depend on the norms of learned parameter matrices; we extend these results to symmetry-constrained equivariant quantum models; and we validate our theoretical framework with numerical experiments. This work provides actionable model design insights and establishes a foundational tool for a more nuanced understanding of generalization in quantum machine learning.

AI.tldr: First PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for quantum models using channel perturbation analysis, providing data-dependent bounds sensitive to learned parameters rather than worst-case capacity.
AI.motivation: Current quantum ML generalization analysis relies on uniform capacity-based bounds that are too loose and insensitive to actual training, lacking non-uniform data-dependent bounds that reflect specific learned solutions.
AI.method: Derived PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for layered quantum circuits composed of general quantum channels (including dissipative operations), using channel perturbation analysis to establish bounds dependent on learned parameter matrix norms, extended to symmetry-constrained equivariant quantum models.
AI.result: Established first non-uniform generalization bounds for quantum models that depend on specific learned parameters rather than worst-case hypothesis class capacity, validated through numerical experiments.
AI.conclusion: Provides actionable model design insights and foundational tools for nuanced understanding of generalization in quantum machine learning, moving beyond loose uniform bounds to data-dependent analysis.

title: Imprecise quantum steering inequalities in tripartite systems
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Comments are welcomed. Accepted by Physical Review A
summary:
Quantum steering, as a manifestation of nonlocal quantum correlations, plays a crucial role in enabling various quantum information processing tasks. However, practical implementations are often hindered by significant challenges arising from imperfect or untrusted measurement devices. This study investigates the impact of measurement inaccuracies on quantum steering, with a particular focus on errors in the untrusted party's measurement devices. We first analyze how such errors affect the evaluation of steering inequalities, and then derive bipartite steering inequalities based on correlation matrices under imperfect measurements.
  Our findings show that even small measurement errors can significantly compromise the certification of quantum steerability, an effect that becomes particularly pronounced as the system dimension increases. Furthermore, by extending the proposed steering inequality to a modified tripartite scenario via correlation matrices, we demonstrate that the influence of measurement imperfections is far more severe in multipartite quantum steering than in the bipartite case. Our results underscore the critical need to account for measurement imperfections in experimental quantum steering and provide a theoretical framework for characterizing and mitigating these effects in high-dimensional quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Measurement imperfections significantly compromise quantum steering certification, with effects worsening in higher dimensions and multipartite scenarios.
AI.motivation: Practical quantum steering implementations face challenges from imperfect/untrusted measurement devices, which hinder quantum information processing tasks.
AI.method: Analyzed measurement inaccuracies' impact on steering inequalities, derived bipartite steering inequalities based on correlation matrices under imperfect measurements, and extended to modified tripartite scenarios.
AI.result: Small measurement errors significantly compromise steerability certification, with effects worsening in higher dimensions; multipartite steering is far more vulnerable to imperfections than bipartite cases.
AI.conclusion: Measurement imperfections must be accounted for in experimental quantum steering; the study provides a theoretical framework for characterizing and mitigating these effects in high-dimensional systems.

title: Dynamical Evolution of Quantum Correlations and Decoherence in Coupled Oscillators Interacting with a Thermal Reservoir
summary: We investigate the dynamical evolution of quantum discord, entanglement and purity in an open quantum system of two coupled asymmetric harmonic oscillators interacting with a thermal environment. Using the Kossakowski-Lindblad master equation we analyze the time evolution starting with a squeezed vacuum state. In contrast to our previous study on entanglement evolution in asymmetric oscillators, the present work introduces XY-type position-position coupling together with a systematic joint analysis of quantum discord and purity alongside entanglement. We examine the combined effects of the squeezing parameter, asymmetry parameter, coupling constant, dissipation rate and temperature. We find that quantum discord and entanglement exhibit, in general, a non-monotonic decrease over time. Increasing temperature consistently accelerates the degradation of both quantum correlations and purity, whereas increasing dissipation accelerates the degradation of quantum correlations but leads to higher steady-state purity. Increasing the squeezing parameter provides a protective effect by enhancing initial correlations and prolonging entanglement survival time, while increasing the coupling constant leads to higher quantum correlations. The asymmetry parameter exhibits only a weak influence on the correlation evolution. Our analysis reveals that quantum discord demonstrates stronger resilience than entanglement, which can present more complex behaviour including entanglement sudden death and possible temporary revivals and re-suppressions. These findings provide valuable insights for developing robust quantum information protocols and strategies for preserving quantum correlations in realistic open quantum systems, with potential extensions to non-Markovian regimes and multi-mode architectures.

AI.tldr: Study of quantum discord, entanglement, and purity dynamics in two coupled asymmetric harmonic oscillators interacting with thermal environment, revealing discord's stronger resilience compared to entanglement.
AI.motivation: To systematically analyze the joint evolution of quantum discord, entanglement, and purity in an open quantum system of coupled asymmetric harmonic oscillators, extending previous work on entanglement alone to include quantum discord and purity, and examining how various parameters affect correlation preservation in realistic quantum systems.
AI.method: Using the Kossakowski-Lindblad master equation to model time evolution starting from a squeezed vacuum state, with XY-type position-position coupling between two asymmetric harmonic oscillators interacting with a thermal environment. Systematic analysis of combined effects of squeezing parameter, asymmetry parameter, coupling constant, dissipation rate, and temperature on quantum discord, entanglement, and purity.
AI.result: Quantum discord and entanglement generally show non-monotonic decrease over time. Temperature increase accelerates degradation of both quantum correlations and purity. Dissipation increase accelerates correlation degradation but leads to higher steady-state purity. Squeezing parameter provides protective effect by enhancing initial correlations and prolonging entanglement survival time. Coupling constant increase leads to higher quantum correlations. Asymmetry parameter has weak influence. Quantum discord demonstrates stronger resilience than entanglement, which exhibits more complex behavior including entanglement sudden death and possible temporary revivals.
AI.conclusion: Quantum discord shows stronger resilience than entanglement in open quantum systems, providing valuable insights for developing robust quantum information protocols and strategies for preserving quantum correlations in realistic environments, with potential extensions to non-Markovian regimes and multi-mode architectures.

title: Connection-topology--dependent energy transport and ergotropy in quantum battery networks with reciprocal and nonreciprocal couplings
summary: The realization of scalable quantum battery architectures requires concern not only with how much energy can be stored, but also with how energy is transported, distributed, and converted into extractable work across connected battery nodes. While previous studies mainly focused on collective charging in multi-cell quantum batteries, the topology-dependent transport law and the corresponding work-oriented performance of quantum battery networks remain largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate quantum battery networks with engineered reciprocal and nonreciprocal couplings and compare different connection topologies, including cascaded and parallel architectures, within a unified transport framework. In the nonreciprocal regime, the optimal coupling follows distinct scaling laws for the two connection topologies, namely $J_{\rm op}^{c}\propto N$ for cascaded transport and $J_{\rm op}^{p}\propto N^{-1/2}$ for parallel charging in the large-$N$ limit. In reciprocal cascaded networks, a parity-dependent spectral response produces an odd-even transport effect that is absent in the nonreciprocal and parallel configurations. We further analyze the role of thermal and squeezed reservoirs and show that thermal noise mainly increases passive energy, whereas squeezing enhances ergotropy and thus the useful fraction of stored energy. These results shift the emphasis from charging enhancement to transport engineering and provide architecture-level design principles for quantum battery networks.

AI.tldr: Quantum battery networks with engineered reciprocal/nonreciprocal couplings show topology-dependent transport laws: cascaded networks require J∝N, parallel networks J∝N⁻¹/² for optimal coupling. Reciprocal cascaded networks exhibit odd-even transport effects. Thermal noise increases passive energy while squeezing enhances extractable work (ergotropy).
AI.motivation: Previous studies focused on collective charging in multi-cell quantum batteries, but topology-dependent transport laws and work-oriented performance of quantum battery networks remain unexplored. Scalable quantum battery architectures require understanding how energy is transported, distributed, and converted into extractable work across connected nodes.
AI.method: Investigate quantum battery networks with engineered reciprocal and nonreciprocal couplings, comparing different connection topologies (cascaded and parallel architectures) within a unified transport framework. Analyze the role of thermal and squeezed reservoirs on energy transport and conversion.
AI.result: Nonreciprocal regime shows distinct scaling laws: optimal coupling J_op^c ∝ N for cascaded transport and J_op^p ∝ N⁻¹/² for parallel charging in large-N limit. Reciprocal cascaded networks exhibit parity-dependent spectral response (odd-even transport effect). Thermal noise mainly increases passive energy, while squeezing enhances ergotropy (useful fraction of stored energy).
AI.conclusion: Results shift emphasis from charging enhancement to transport engineering, providing architecture-level design principles for quantum battery networks. Different topologies require different coupling strategies, and reservoir engineering (squeezing) can enhance extractable work, offering practical guidelines for scalable quantum battery design.

title: Local and Global Master Equations through the Lens of Non-Hermitian Physics
comment: 11 pages with 7 figures, appendices with 3 figures
summary: We investigate the relation between non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and Lindblad dynamics in nonequilibrium open quantum systems. Non-Hermitian models can extend phase diagrams and enable sensing advantages, but such effects often rely on postselection, raising questions about their relevance for unconditional dynamics. Using a minimal two-qubit setup mediating a heat current, we compare local and global Markovian master equations with their non-Hermitian counterparts. We observe that exceptional points emerge only in the local master equation and in the corresponding non-Hermitian Hamiltonian at sufficiently strong nonequilibrium. We further consider hybrid configurations, where one bath is treated with a Lindblad description and the other with a non-Hermitian approach, interpolating between the two extremes. Our results contribute understanding the role of quantum jumps and exceptional points in nonequilibrium open quantum systems and identify a simple, experimentally accessible architecture, realizable, for instance, in circuit-QED platforms, for their exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the relationship between non-Hermitian Hamiltonians and Lindblad dynamics in open quantum systems, showing that exceptional points emerge only in local master equations and their non-Hermitian counterparts under strong nonequilibrium conditions.
AI.motivation: To understand the connection between non-Hermitian Hamiltonian models and Lindblad dynamics in nonequilibrium open quantum systems, particularly addressing whether non-Hermitian effects (like exceptional points) that rely on postselection are relevant for unconditional dynamics.
AI.method: Uses a minimal two-qubit setup mediating a heat current to compare local and global Markovian master equations with their non-Hermitian counterparts. Also considers hybrid configurations where one bath is treated with Lindblad description and the other with non-Hermitian approach.
AI.result: Exceptional points emerge only in the local master equation and in the corresponding non-Hermitian Hamiltonian at sufficiently strong nonequilibrium. The hybrid configurations interpolate between the two extremes.
AI.conclusion: The results contribute to understanding the role of quantum jumps and exceptional points in nonequilibrium open quantum systems and identify a simple, experimentally accessible architecture (e.g., circuit-QED platforms) for exploring these phenomena.

title: Zero-Uncertainty States Relative to Observable Algebras
summary: We study zero-uncertainty states with quantum memory from an operator-algebraic perspective, which naturally accommodates degenerate projective-valued measurements. In the equal-dimension setting, we prove a rigidity theorem for purity and maximal entanglement. We then analyze two mechanisms by which this rigidity can fail: one arising from proper observable subalgebras, and the other from allowing larger memory dimensions. In these cases, we give corresponding algebraic decomposition and representation-theoretic descriptions, and compare their mathematical structure with their physical interpretation. Finally, we present an example from quantum steering to illustrate how our framework helps resolve a concrete physical question in a specific setting.

AI.tldr: Operator-algebraic analysis of zero-uncertainty states with quantum memory, including rigidity theorems for purity/maximal entanglement and mechanisms for rigidity failure.
AI.motivation: To develop a comprehensive operator-algebraic framework for studying zero-uncertainty states with quantum memory that naturally handles degenerate projective-valued measurements, which traditional approaches may not accommodate well.
AI.method: Operator-algebraic perspective with von Neumann algebras to analyze zero-uncertainty states; proves rigidity theorem for equal-dimension case; examines two failure mechanisms (observable subalgebras and larger memory dimensions) with algebraic decomposition and representation-theoretic descriptions.
AI.result: Established a rigidity theorem showing purity and maximal entanglement in equal-dimension setting; identified and characterized two mechanisms where rigidity fails; provided mathematical structure-physical interpretation comparisons; demonstrated framework's utility through quantum steering example.
AI.conclusion: The operator-algebraic framework provides a natural and powerful approach to study zero-uncertainty states with quantum memory, offering mathematical rigor, handling degeneracy naturally, and yielding concrete physical insights applicable to problems like quantum steering.

title: Bell Experiments Revisited: A Numerical Approach Based on De Broglie--Bohm Theory
summary: We present a complete and rigorous model of an EPR--Bell-type experiment within the framework of the de Broglie--Bohm theory. The purpose of this work is to show explicitly how a deterministic hidden-variable theory can reproduce all quantum-mechanical predictions, including the violation of Bell inequalities. Combining analytical arguments with numerical simulations, our approach offers a unified and transparent illustration of the central ingredients of de Broglie--Bohm theory, including particle trajectories, spin dynamics, and quantum entanglement. The model is designed to be pedagogical and self-contained, making it suitable for readers seeking a concrete understanding of how a nonlocal hidden-variable theory can describe the EPR--Bell experiment and illustrate Bell's theorem.

AI.tldr: A complete de Broglie-Bohm model of EPR-Bell experiments showing how deterministic hidden variables reproduce quantum predictions including Bell inequality violations.
AI.motivation: To explicitly demonstrate how a deterministic hidden-variable theory (de Broglie-Bohm) can reproduce all quantum-mechanical predictions, including Bell inequality violations, and provide a pedagogical illustration of the theory's key elements.
AI.method: Developed a complete and rigorous model of EPR-Bell experiments within de Broglie-Bohm framework, combining analytical arguments with numerical simulations to illustrate particle trajectories, spin dynamics, and quantum entanglement.
AI.result: The model successfully shows how de Broglie-Bohm theory can reproduce all quantum predictions, including violation of Bell inequalities, through explicit demonstration of nonlocal hidden-variable dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a concrete, pedagogical demonstration that deterministic hidden-variable theories (specifically de Broglie-Bohm) can fully account for quantum phenomena in EPR-Bell experiments, illustrating Bell's theorem through explicit modeling of nonlocal interactions.

title: Propagation of optical vector vortices of slow light in a coherently prepared tripod configuration
summary: We investigate the propagation of optical vector vortices of slow light in a coherently prepared four-level tripod atomic system. The vector vortex consists of superposed pulse pairs with opposite circular polarizations and orbital angular momentum (OAM) charges $\pm l$, weakly interacting with an atomic medium initially prepared in a coherent superposition of two ground states. A third unoccupied state is coupled to a stronger control laser without OAM, creating a phase-dependent configuration. In the linear regime, the vortex OAM is mapped onto the medium, producing symmetrical azimuthally structured absorption patterns, with losses significantly reduced by the control field. For small detunings, complementary spatially dependent amplification and absorption occur for the two circular polarization components. This OAM-structured coherence induces a dynamical anisotropy, affecting both the intensity and polarization of the slow-light vortex. Polarization states evolve periodically between left-circular, linear, and right-circular polarizations during propagation. Once the beam reaches a stationary regime, the ring-shaped intensity transforms into a petal-like structure, and the final polarization states stabilize according to the initial superposition. The rate of polarization transitions is tunable via the control field strength, demonstrating flexible control over slow-light vector vortex dynamics.

AI.tldr: Optical vector vortices of slow light propagate in a four-level tripod atomic system, with OAM mapping onto the medium creating structured absorption/amplification patterns and tunable polarization dynamics.
AI.motivation: To investigate how optical vector vortices (superposed pulse pairs with opposite circular polarizations and OAM charges) propagate in coherently prepared atomic media, particularly focusing on how vortex OAM interacts with atomic coherence and how this affects polarization dynamics of slow light.
AI.method: Use a four-level tripod atomic system with two ground states prepared in coherent superposition, a third unoccupied state coupled to a stronger control laser without OAM, and vector vortex beams (superposed pulse pairs with opposite circular polarizations and OAM charges ±l) weakly interacting with the medium in the linear regime.
AI.result: Vortex OAM maps onto the medium creating symmetrical azimuthally structured absorption patterns with reduced losses; small detunings produce complementary spatially dependent amplification/absorption for polarization components; OAM-structured coherence induces dynamical anisotropy affecting intensity and polarization; polarization evolves periodically between left-circular, linear, and right-circular states; stationary regime transforms ring-shaped intensity into petal-like structure with stabilized polarization states; polarization transition rate is tunable via control field strength.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates flexible control over slow-light vector vortex dynamics through tunable polarization transitions and structured absorption/amplification patterns, showing how OAM-structured coherence in atomic media can manipulate both intensity and polarization evolution of optical vortices.

title: Metastability, chaos and spectrum tomography for Bose-Hubbard rings and chains
summary: We analyze the metastability of Bose-Hubbard condensates for finite-size one-dimensional ring lattices and open chains, using a semiclassical tomographic perspective that emphasizes the relation of the many-body spectrum to the underlying classical phase-space structures. This constitutes an arena for inspection of quantum ergodicity and localization, in far-from-equilibrium scenarios of experimental interest. Both local aspects (via Bogoliubov analysis) and global aspects (by inspecting the mixed regular-chaotic dynamics) are addressed. We also clarify how chaos is diminished in the limit of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation.

AI.tldr: Semiclassical analysis of Bose-Hubbard condensates in 1D ring lattices and chains reveals connections between many-body spectra and classical phase-space structures, examining quantum ergodicity, localization, and chaos suppression in Gross-Pitaevskii limit.
AI.motivation: To understand metastability of Bose-Hubbard condensates in finite-size 1D systems using semiclassical methods, providing insights into quantum ergodicity and localization in far-from-equilibrium experimental scenarios.
AI.method: Semiclassical tomographic approach relating many-body spectrum to classical phase-space structures; local analysis via Bogoliubov theory; global analysis by examining mixed regular-chaotic dynamics; investigation of chaos suppression in Gross-Pitaevskii limit.
AI.result: Establishes connections between quantum many-body spectra and classical phase-space structures; reveals how chaos diminishes in the Gross-Pitaevskii equation limit; provides framework for analyzing quantum ergodicity and localization in Bose-Hubbard systems.
AI.conclusion: Semiclassical tomographic perspective effectively links quantum many-body physics to classical phase-space structures, offering insights into metastability, ergodicity, and chaos in Bose-Hubbard condensates, with implications for understanding far-from-equilibrium quantum dynamics.

title: Quantum speedup from nonclassical polarization
summary: We develop a framework for identifying nonclassical speedups in systems with polarization, likewise spin degrees of freedom. By confining the dynamics to the manifold of angular momentum coherent states, which act as the classical reference in this case, we compute the speed limit that bounds the rate of change of the state achievable without generating quantum coherence. A comparison with the unrestricted quantum speed limit enables the quantitative identification of speedups arising from polarization nonclassicality. We apply this framework to the cross-Kerr interaction, demonstrating a persistent speedup scaling as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$ with the photon number $N$. The results establish polarization nonclassicality as a genuine dynamical resource, linking quantum coherence to quantum-enhanced evolution speeds in nonlinear photonic systems.

AI.tldr: Framework identifies quantum speedups from polarization nonclassicality by comparing speed limits with and without quantum coherence generation, showing O(√N) scaling in cross-Kerr systems.
AI.motivation: To establish polarization nonclassicality as a genuine dynamical resource by quantitatively identifying speedups arising from quantum coherence in systems with polarization/spin degrees of freedom.
AI.method: Confine dynamics to angular momentum coherent states (classical reference), compute speed limit without coherence generation, compare with unrestricted quantum speed limit to identify quantum speedups.
AI.result: Demonstrated persistent speedup scaling as O(√N) with photon number N in cross-Kerr interaction, quantitatively showing polarization nonclassicality enables faster evolution.
AI.conclusion: Polarization nonclassicality is a genuine dynamical resource that links quantum coherence to quantum-enhanced evolution speeds in nonlinear photonic systems.

title: Block Coordinate Descent for Dynamic Portfolio Optimization on Finite-Precision Coherent Ising Machines
summary: Coherent Ising machines (CIMs) have emerged as specialized quantum hardware for large-scale combinatorial optimization. However, for large instances that remain challenging for classical methods, some platforms support only finite-precision inputs, and the required scaling and quantization can degrade solution quality. Dynamic portfolio optimization (DPO) can be formulated as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem, but large instances are especially vulnerable to precision loss under global scaling. We propose a block coordinate descent method that decomposes the DPO model along the time dimension and iteratively solves compact time-block subproblems on the device. Experiments on finite-precision CIM hardware show that the method enables these instances to be solved under hardware precision limits, yields portfolios competitive with classical benchmark solvers, and reduces runtime through fast CIM solution of the resulting subproblems. These results demonstrate the promise of finite-precision CIMs as a practical and scalable approach to structured large-scale combinatorial optimization.

AI.tldr: Block coordinate descent method enables dynamic portfolio optimization on finite-precision coherent Ising machines by decomposing large QUBO problems into time-block subproblems that fit hardware precision limits.
AI.motivation: Large-scale combinatorial optimization problems like dynamic portfolio optimization (DPO) can be formulated as QUBO problems, but finite-precision CIM hardware struggles with global scaling of large instances, leading to precision loss and degraded solution quality.
AI.method: Proposes a block coordinate descent method that decomposes the DPO model along the time dimension, iteratively solving compact time-block subproblems on the finite-precision CIM device to overcome hardware precision limits.
AI.result: Experiments show the method enables solving DPO instances under hardware precision limits, yields portfolios competitive with classical benchmark solvers, and reduces runtime through fast CIM solution of subproblems.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates the promise of finite-precision CIMs as a practical and scalable method for structured large-scale combinatorial optimization problems like dynamic portfolio optimization.

title: Solving Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations via a Hybrid Newton Method Using Quantum Linear System Solver
comment: 24 pages, 18 figures, submitted to SIAM Journal on Scientifc Computing
summary: To approximate solutions of complex nonlinear partial differential equations remains a computational challenge, especially for sets of equations relevant in industry, such as Euler or Navier-Stokes equations. Even the most sophisticated computational fluid dynamic algorithms coupled with powerful supercomputers can not find approximate solutions for several design challenges in both adequate time and scale-resolving accuracy. One difficulty arises from solving high dimensional, strongly nonlinear partial differential equations, such as the Navier-Stokes equations, which capture the underlying physics. For nearly all classical algorithms, methods closely related to Newton's method are used to approximate a solution to the problem. Approximately solving the large-scale linear systems of equations occurring in this iterative scheme is generally a main contributor to the total computational complexity. In this paper a new quantum linear system solver supporting Newton's classical method to solve nonlinear partial differential equations is introduced. We present a new variant of the HHL algorithm, requiring less apriori information regarding the eigenvalues of the corresponding matrix. We apply this quantum linear system solver in a hybrid quantum-classical fashion to solve nonlinear partial differential equations. Moreover, a resource estimation for advanced use-cases of practical relevance is provided. Our results demonstrate how quantum computation may improve existing classical methodologies for solving nonlinear partial differential equations. This approach provides another promising application of quantum computers and presents a possible way forward for handling nonlinearities on inherently linear quantum systems.

AI.tldr: A quantum-classical hybrid approach using a modified HHL algorithm to solve nonlinear PDEs like Navier-Stokes, requiring less eigenvalue information than standard quantum linear solvers.
AI.motivation: Solving complex nonlinear PDEs (Euler, Navier-Stokes) remains computationally challenging for industrial applications; classical Newton-based methods require solving large linear systems that dominate computational complexity.
AI.method: A new variant of the HHL quantum linear system solver requiring less a priori eigenvalue information, applied in hybrid quantum-classical fashion within Newton's method for nonlinear PDEs.
AI.result: Resource estimation for practical use-cases demonstrates how quantum computation can improve classical methodologies for solving nonlinear PDEs.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a promising application of quantum computers and a potential pathway for handling nonlinearities on inherently linear quantum systems.

title: Traveling Salesman Problem with a preprocessing method for classical and quantum optimization
summary: The Traveling Salesman Problem is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem widely studied in operations research. Despite its simple formulation, it remains computationally challenging due to the exponential growth of the search space and the large number of constraints required to eliminate subtours. This paper introduces a preprocessing strategy that significantly reduces the size of the optimization model by restricting the set of candidate arcs and retaining only the lowest-cost neighbors for each vertex. Computational experiments on TSPLIB benchmark instances demonstrate that the proposed approach substantially reduces the number of decision variables. The method is evaluated using both classical and quantum optimization techniques, showing improvements in computational time and reductions in optimality gaps. Overall, the results indicate that the proposed preprocessing enhances the scalability of the formulations and makes them more suitable for both classical solvers and emerging quantum optimization frameworks.

AI.tldr: A preprocessing strategy for TSP that reduces model size by restricting candidate arcs to lowest-cost neighbors, improving scalability for both classical and quantum optimization.
AI.motivation: The Traveling Salesman Problem is computationally challenging due to exponential search space growth and numerous constraints needed to eliminate subtours. There's a need for methods that reduce model complexity to make TSP more tractable for both classical and emerging quantum optimization approaches.
AI.method: Introduces a preprocessing strategy that significantly reduces optimization model size by restricting the set of candidate arcs and retaining only the lowest-cost neighbors for each vertex. This reduces the number of decision variables in the formulation.
AI.result: Computational experiments on TSPLIB benchmark instances show substantial reduction in decision variables. The method improves computational time and reduces optimality gaps when evaluated with both classical and quantum optimization techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed preprocessing enhances the scalability of TSP formulations, making them more suitable for both classical solvers and emerging quantum optimization frameworks by reducing model complexity while maintaining solution quality.

title: Global control via quantum actuators
summary: We introduce the concept of quantum actuators as mediators for globally controlled quantum computation. Auxiliary quantum systems act as controllable elements that transiently store and release interaction energy, enabling the selective activation of multi-qubit gates within globally driven architectures. During compilation they remain passive and require no fine-grained local control, while during operation they allow for controlled activation of interactions and directional flow of quantum information. We provide a framework for embedding quantum actuators in globally controlled processors, showing how they enhance connectivity, enable long-range entangling operations, and bridge distant regions without increasing local control overhead. We discuss physical implementations and architectural strategies illustrating how these elements extend the capabilities of global-control schemes. A complementary interpretation in terms of quantum batteries naturally emerges, connecting global-control architectures with concepts from quantum thermodynamics while highlighting the distinct operational role of quantum actuators.

AI.tldr: Quantum actuators are auxiliary systems that enable selective multi-qubit gate activation in globally controlled quantum processors without requiring fine-grained local control.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of globally controlled quantum architectures by enabling selective activation of interactions and directional information flow without increasing local control overhead.
AI.method: Introduce quantum actuators as controllable elements that transiently store and release interaction energy, providing a framework for embedding them in globally controlled processors to enhance connectivity and enable long-range operations.
AI.result: Quantum actuators enhance connectivity, enable long-range entangling operations, bridge distant regions, and provide a complementary interpretation as quantum batteries connecting global-control architectures with quantum thermodynamics.
AI.conclusion: Quantum actuators extend capabilities of global-control schemes by mediating computation, enabling selective gate activation while maintaining passive operation during compilation, with natural connections to quantum battery concepts.

title: Two-parameter Family-Vicsek scaling in a dissipative XXZ spin chain
summary: Family-Vicsek (FV) scaling provides an understanding for the growth and finite-size saturation of fluctuations in classical systems. Here, we extend the FV roughness to transferred segment magnetization after quantum quenches in a dissipative XXZ spin chain with homogeneous gain and loss, starting from a nonequilibrium steady state with finite magnetization. In the non-interacting limit, we derive a closed-form expression for the roughness in the presence of dissipation. It displays two-parameter FV scaling and smoothly interpolates between the clean ballistic behavior and the dissipation dominated scalings. For interacting chains, tensor-network simulations show that the non-dissipative ballistic growth at finite magnetization is robust, whereas the full Lindblad evolution is generically controlled by the dissipative relaxation time and exhibits a dissipation-dominated collapse.

AI.tldr: Extends Family-Vicsek scaling to quantum quenches in dissipative XXZ spin chains, showing how dissipation affects roughness scaling of transferred segment magnetization.
AI.motivation: To extend classical Family-Vicsek scaling concepts to quantum systems with dissipation, specifically examining how quantum quenches in dissipative spin chains affect roughness scaling of magnetization.
AI.method: For non-interacting limit: derived closed-form expression for roughness with dissipation. For interacting chains: used tensor-network simulations to study Lindblad evolution and dissipative effects.
AI.result: Non-interacting case shows two-parameter FV scaling interpolating between clean ballistic and dissipation-dominated regimes. Interacting chains show robust ballistic growth at finite magnetization without dissipation, but dissipative relaxation dominates Lindblad evolution.
AI.conclusion: Family-Vicsek scaling can be extended to quantum dissipative systems, with dissipation controlling the scaling behavior and causing collapse to dissipation-dominated regimes in interacting systems.

title: Encoding Numerical Data for Generative Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Generative quantum machine learning models are trained to deduce the probability distribution underlying a given dataset, and to produce new, synthetic samples from it. The majority of such models proposed in the literature, like the Quantum Circuit Born Machine (QCBM), fundamentally work on a binary level. Real-world data, however, is often numeric, requiring the models to translate between binary and continuous representations. We analyze how this transition influences the performance of quantum models and show that it requires the models to learn correlations that are solely an artifact of the way the data is encoded, and not related to the data itself. At the same time, structure of the original data can be obscured in the binary representation, hindering generalization. To mitigate these effects, we propose a strategy based on Gray-codes that can be implemented with essentially no overhead, conserves structures in the data, and avoids artificial correlations in situations in which the standard approach creates them. Considering datasets drawn from various one-dimensional probability distributions, we verify that, in most cases, QCBMs using the reflected Gray code learn faster and more accurately than those with standard binary code.

AI.tldr: Quantum machine learning models like QCBM typically use binary encoding for continuous data, which introduces artificial correlations and obscures data structure. Using Gray codes instead improves learning speed and accuracy by preserving structure and avoiding encoding artifacts.
AI.motivation: Real-world data is often continuous/numeric, but quantum generative models like QCBM work on binary representations. The binary encoding process introduces artificial correlations unrelated to the actual data and obscures the original data structure, hindering model generalization and performance.
AI.method: Proposed using Gray codes (specifically reflected Gray code) instead of standard binary encoding for converting continuous data to binary representation in quantum models. This approach has essentially no overhead, conserves data structures, and avoids artificial correlations introduced by standard binary encoding.
AI.result: Experiments with datasets from various one-dimensional probability distributions show that QCBMs using reflected Gray code learn faster and more accurately than those with standard binary code in most cases.
AI.conclusion: The choice of binary encoding significantly impacts quantum generative model performance. Gray codes provide a superior alternative to standard binary encoding by preserving data structure and avoiding encoding-induced artifacts, leading to improved learning efficiency and accuracy.

title: Single-letter one-way distillable entanglement for non-degradable states
summary:
The one-way distillable entanglement is a central operational measure of bipartite entanglement, quantifying the optimal rate at which maximally entangled pairs can be extracted by one-way LOCC. Despite its importance, it is notoriously hard to compute, since it is defined by a regularized optimization over many copies and adaptive one-way protocols. At present, single-letter formulas are only known for (conjugate) degradable and PPT states. More generally, it has remained unclear when one-way distillable entanglement can still be additive beyond degradability and PPT settings, and how such additivity relates to additivity questions of quantum capacity of channels.
  In this paper, we address this gap by identifying three explicit families of non-degradable and non-PPT states whose one-way distillable entanglement is nevertheless single-letter. First, we introduce two weakened degradability-type conditions--regularized less-noisy and informationally degradable--and prove that each guarantees additivity and hence a single-letter formula. Second, we show a stability result for orthogonally flagged mixtures: when one component has orthogonal support on Alice's system and zero one-way distillable entanglement, the mixture remains single-letter, even though degradability is typically lost under such mixing. Finally, we propose a generalized spin-alignment principle for entropy minimization in tensor-product settings, which we establish in several key cases, including a complete Rényi-2 result. As an application, we obtain additivity results for generalized direct-sum channels and their corresponding Choi states.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies three families of non-degradable, non-PPT states with single-letter one-way distillable entanglement formulas, introduces weakened degradability conditions, shows stability for orthogonally flagged mixtures, and develops a generalized spin-alignment principle for entropy minimization.
AI.motivation: One-way distillable entanglement is a fundamental operational measure but notoriously hard to compute, with single-letter formulas only known for degradable and PPT states. There's a gap in understanding when additivity holds beyond these settings and how it relates to channel capacity additivity.
AI.method: 1) Introduce two weakened degradability-type conditions (regularized less-noisy and informationally degradable) proving each guarantees additivity. 2) Show stability for orthogonally flagged mixtures where one component has orthogonal support on Alice's system and zero one-way distillable entanglement. 3) Propose a generalized spin-alignment principle for entropy minimization in tensor-product settings, establishing it in key cases including complete Rényi-2 results.
AI.result: The paper obtains explicit families of non-degradable, non-PPT states with single-letter one-way distillable entanglement formulas, provides additivity results for generalized direct-sum channels and their corresponding Choi states, and establishes new conditions under which additivity holds beyond previously known settings.
AI.conclusion: The work addresses the computational gap for one-way distillable entanglement by identifying new families of states with single-letter formulas, introducing weakened degradability conditions, and developing techniques for entropy minimization that enable additivity proofs beyond degradable and PPT settings.

title: Quantum simulation of Motzkin spin chain with Rydberg atoms
summary: Motzkin spin chain is a well-known mathematical model with connections to symmetry-protected topological phases, such as the Haldane phase, as well as to concepts in the AdS/CFT correspondence. They exhibit highly entangled ground states that violate the area law and are exceptionally difficult to simulate with conventional numerical methods. Numerical simulations of the Motzkin ground state become further challenging at large system sizes due to their high-dimensional spin structure, rendering it a natural test bed for quantum simulation with ultra-cold systems. Here, we propose a Rydberg-atom based quantum simulation scheme that effectively realizes Motzkin spins using an experimentally accessible set of parameters. We show that the resulting effective Motzkin ground state reproduces the characteristic entanglement scaling and the block-structure properties of the reduced density matrix associated with the ideal Motzkin state. Our results establish a pathway toward a concrete experimental realization of Motzkin spins beyond purely mathematical constructions, opening avenues for exploring other similar exotic non-area-law entangled phases in programmable Rydberg simulators.

AI.tldr: Rydberg-atom quantum simulation scheme for Motzkin spin chain ground state, reproducing entanglement scaling and density matrix properties.
AI.motivation: Motzkin spin chains exhibit highly entangled ground states violating area law, are difficult to simulate numerically, and serve as test bed for quantum simulation with ultra-cold systems.
AI.method: Proposed Rydberg-atom based quantum simulation scheme using experimentally accessible parameters to effectively realize Motzkin spins.
AI.result: Effective Motzkin ground state reproduces characteristic entanglement scaling and block-structure properties of reduced density matrix associated with ideal Motzkin state.
AI.conclusion: Establishes pathway toward experimental realization of Motzkin spins beyond mathematical constructions, enabling exploration of exotic non-area-law entangled phases in programmable Rydberg simulators.

title: Tensor network influence functionals for open quantum systems with general Gaussian bosonic baths
summary: Dynamics of open quantum systems with structured reservoirs can often be simulated efficiently with tensor network influence functionals. The standard variants of the time-evolving matrix product operator (TEMPO) method are applicable when the systems is coupled to Gaussian bosonic baths via hermitian coupling operators that mutually commute. In this work we introduce a generalization to cases where the system is coupled to a single reservoir through multiple non-commuting operators, representing the most general form of linear system-bath coupling. We construct a Gaussian influence functional that properly handles Trotter errors arising from a finite evolution time step, thus ensuring convergence for long evolution times. Based on this result, the uniform TEMPO scheme can be employed to obtain a matrix product operator form of the influence functional, enabling efficient simulations of the real-time dynamics of the open system. As a demonstration, we simulate the time evolution of driven two-level emitters coupled to a bosonic lattice at different lattice sites.

AI.tldr: Generalization of TEMPO method to handle non-commuting coupling operators in open quantum systems with structured reservoirs.
AI.motivation: Standard TEMPO methods are limited to Gaussian bosonic baths with hermitian coupling operators that mutually commute, but many realistic systems involve non-commuting operators representing the most general form of linear system-bath coupling.
AI.method: Constructed a Gaussian influence functional that properly handles Trotter errors from finite evolution time steps, enabling convergence for long evolution times. Applied uniform TEMPO scheme to obtain matrix product operator form of the influence functional.
AI.result: Developed a generalized TEMPO method applicable to systems coupled to single reservoirs through multiple non-commuting operators. Demonstrated the method by simulating time evolution of driven two-level emitters coupled to bosonic lattices at different sites.
AI.conclusion: The generalized TEMPO method enables efficient simulations of real-time dynamics for open quantum systems with the most general linear system-bath coupling, overcoming limitations of previous approaches that required commuting coupling operators.

title: Scalable quantum circuit generation for iterative ground state approximation using Majorana Propagation
summary: We introduce the Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter ansatz Variational Majorana Propagation Eigensolver (ADAPT-VMPE), a quantum-inspired classical algorithm that exploits Majorana Propagation (MP) to produce circuits for approximating the ground state of molecular Hamiltonians. Equipped with the theoretical guarantees of MP, which provide controllable bounds on the approximation error, ADAPT-VMPE offers an efficient and scalable approach for iterative ansatz construction. A theoretical analysis of the computational complexity demonstrates that it is polynomial in both the number of qubits and the number of iterations. We present an in-depth analysis of circuit construction strategies, analyzing their impact on convergence and provide practical guidance for efficient ansatz generation. Using ADAPT-VMPE, we construct up to 100-qubit ansätze for a strongly correlated photosensitizer currently undergoing human clinical trials for cancer treatment. Our results demonstrate that constant overlap with the ground state across system sizes can be reached in polynomial time with polynomially sized circuits.

AI.tldr: ADAPT-VMPE is a quantum-inspired classical algorithm that uses Majorana Propagation to construct variational ansätze for approximating molecular ground states with polynomial complexity in qubits and iterations.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient and scalable approach for constructing quantum circuits that approximate ground states of molecular Hamiltonians, particularly for strongly correlated systems like photosensitizers used in cancer treatment, with theoretical guarantees on approximation error.
AI.method: Adaptive Derivative-Assembled Pseudo-Trotter ansatz Variational Majorana Propagation Eigensolver (ADAPT-VMPE) exploits Majorana Propagation (MP) to iteratively construct ansätze. The method uses theoretical guarantees of MP for controllable error bounds and analyzes circuit construction strategies for efficient ansatz generation.
AI.result: The algorithm demonstrates polynomial computational complexity in both number of qubits and iterations. Constructed up to 100-qubit ansätze for a strongly correlated photosensitizer in clinical trials for cancer treatment, achieving constant overlap with ground state across system sizes in polynomial time with polynomially sized circuits.
AI.conclusion: ADAPT-VMPE provides an efficient, scalable quantum-inspired classical approach for molecular ground state approximation with theoretical error guarantees, enabling practical application to large-scale strongly correlated systems relevant to medical applications.

title: Information-Theoretic Scaling Laws of Neural Quantum States
summary: We establish an information-theoretic scaling law for generic autoregressive neural quantum states, determined by the middle-cut mutual information of the wavefunction amplitude. By formalizing the virtual bond as an effective information channel across a sequence bipartition, we rigorously prove that exact autoregressive representation of a quantum state requires the virtual-bond dimension to scale with the amplitude mutual information. For stabilizer-state families, we show that this law yields an explicit, analytical rank formula. Applying this framework across quantum-state tomography, ground-state and finite-temperature learning, our numerical experiments expose precise exponent matching, architecture-dependent scaling differences between recurrent and Transformer neural quantum state, and the critical role of autoregressive basis ordering. These results establish a rigorous physical link between the intrinsic structure of a quantum many-body state and the corresponding neural-network capacity required for its faithful representation.

AI.tldr: Information-theoretic scaling law for autoregressive neural quantum states shows virtual-bond dimension must scale with amplitude mutual information, with applications to tomography and state learning.
AI.motivation: To establish a rigorous physical link between the intrinsic structure of quantum many-body states and the neural-network capacity required for their faithful representation, bridging information theory and neural quantum state representations.
AI.method: Formalize virtual bond as effective information channel across sequence bipartition, prove scaling law for virtual-bond dimension with amplitude mutual information, derive analytical rank formula for stabilizer states, and conduct numerical experiments across quantum-state tomography, ground-state and finite-temperature learning.
AI.result: Proved exact autoregressive representation requires virtual-bond dimension scaling with amplitude mutual information; derived explicit analytical rank formula for stabilizer-state families; numerical experiments show precise exponent matching, architecture-dependent scaling differences between recurrent and Transformer neural quantum states, and critical role of autoregressive basis ordering.
AI.conclusion: Established rigorous information-theoretic scaling law linking quantum state structure to neural-network capacity requirements, providing fundamental limits for autoregressive neural quantum state representations with implications for quantum state tomography and learning.

title: Initial State Memory in Finite Random Brickwork Circuits
summary: We ask under what conditions a finite brickwork circuit of random gates retains local information about the initial state. To answer this question we measure the averaged Frobenius distance between the reduced states obtained by evolving two arbitrary initial states and tracing out a portion of the system. By characterising this distance exactly at all times we find that the information is retained if the environment -- the subsystem traced out -- is smaller than half of the system and washed away otherwise. We also find that, while the dynamics of the Frobenius distance depends on the specific initial states chosen, this dependence becomes increasingly weak for large scales and eventually the Frobenius distance attains a universal form as a function of time. Finally, we show that by introducing weak enough boundary dissipation, one can observe a phase transition between a memory preserving phase and one where the information is completely lost.

AI.tldr: Finite brickwork circuits of random gates retain local information when environment is smaller than half the system, with universal dynamics at large scales and phase transitions under weak boundary dissipation.
AI.motivation: To understand conditions under which finite brickwork circuits of random gates preserve local information about initial states, and how this depends on system-environment partitioning.
AI.method: Analyze averaged Frobenius distance between reduced states from evolving two arbitrary initial states and tracing out subsystems; characterize distance exactly at all times; examine dependence on initial states and scale; introduce weak boundary dissipation.
AI.result: Information retained when environment (traced-out subsystem) is smaller than half the system, lost otherwise; Frobenius distance becomes universal at large scales; weak boundary dissipation induces phase transition between memory-preserving and information-lost phases.
AI.conclusion: Finite random circuits exhibit threshold behavior for information retention based on environment size, with universal large-scale dynamics and dissipation-induced phase transitions in memory preservation.
